title: Data Analytics and Information Systems
courseDescription: Introduces how businesses use information systems and data to make better decisions. Students work with spreadsheets, databases, and data visualizations to collect, explore, organize, and present information while examining how technology supports business strategy and operations.
whyRecommended: Builds practical data and technology skills that are useful across analytics, information systems, business intelligence, consulting, and other data-driven careers.

title: Data Management and Database Systems
courseDescription: Introduces how relational databases are designed, built, and managed. Students learn to organize data, create database structures, write SQL queries, and work with systems such as Microsoft Access and Oracle while considering how organizations manage data as a valuable business resource.
whyRecommended: Builds practical database and SQL skills used in data analytics, information systems, software, and business intelligence careers.

title: Data Visualization
courseDescription: Teaches students how to turn complex datasets into clear and useful visual information. Students clean and prepare real-world data, choose appropriate ways to present it, and create charts, maps, heatmaps, dashboards, and other visualizations using tools such as Tableau, Python, and R.
whyRecommended: Develops the ability to communicate data clearly and turn analysis into visual insights for technical and non-technical audiences.

title: Aquatic Ecology
courseDescription: Examines the ecology of aquatic environments and the organisms that live within them. Students use field-based methods to study aquatic ecosystems, collect environmental samples, and explore how biological and environmental factors affect ecosystem health.
whyRecommended: Provides hands-on ecological field experience for students interested in environmental science, conservation, biology, and ecosystem research.

title: Acting I
courseDescription: Introduces the fundamentals of acting through scene work and exercises involving movement, voice, concentration, imagination, improvisation, emotion, and expression. Students learn how to analyze characters and prepare scenes for performance.
whyRecommended: Develops performance, communication, confidence, improvisation, and character-analysis skills useful in theatre and other presentation-focused careers.

title: Acting II
courseDescription: Builds on introductory acting skills through advanced scene work, monologues, and performance techniques drawn from different historical styles. Students develop greater control, range, and flexibility as performers.
whyRecommended: Strengthens advanced acting and performance skills for students interested in professional theatre, directing, film, or other performance-based careers.
prerequisites: DR 350 or audition with theatre faculty

title: Adolescent Development
courseDescription: Examines the physical, cognitive, emotional, and social changes that occur during adolescence. Students explore major theories of adolescent development and how family, peers, culture, and other environmental influences shape adolescent behavior and personality.
whyRecommended: Builds a deeper understanding of adolescent behavior and development for careers involving psychology, counseling, education, youth services, and human development.

title: Adult Development
courseDescription: Examines how people change from young adulthood through later life, including physical, cognitive, emotional, and social development. Students explore how relationships, culture, environment, and life experiences influence development across adulthood.
whyRecommended: Builds an understanding of adult behavior and development that is useful in psychology, counseling, healthcare, research, and other people-focused careers.

title: Advertising Copy Writing
courseDescription: Develops practical skills for creating persuasive advertising messages across different media. Students practice writing advertising copy, developing creative concepts, and turning campaign strategies into clear and engaging content.
whyRecommended: Builds persuasive writing and creative campaign skills for careers in advertising, branding, marketing, and content creation.

title: Advertising Management
courseDescription: Examines how advertising campaigns are planned and managed from a business perspective. Students learn about account management, advertising strategy, campaign budgeting, media planning, and selecting where and how advertisements are placed.
whyRecommended: Develops the strategic and business side of advertising for students interested in campaign management, media planning, marketing, and brand strategy.

title: African American History through Film
courseDescription: Explores major events, people, and themes in African American history through film, historical readings, and primary sources. Students examine both the history being portrayed and how films interpret and represent the African American experience.
whyRecommended: Strengthens historical analysis, cultural understanding, and media interpretation for students interested in history, film, journalism, education, public policy, and cultural research.

title: Algorithm Analysis
courseDescription: Studies how algorithms are designed, evaluated, and compared for efficiency. Students work with techniques such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, shortest-path methods, and computational complexity.
whyRecommended: Strengthens advanced problem-solving and algorithm design skills used in software engineering, machine learning, quantitative development, and other computing careers.
prerequisites: CS 295 or MA 295 or MA 395 or equivalent course

title: American Politics
courseDescription: Introduces the American political system, including Congress, the presidency, the courts, political parties, interest groups, elections, public policy, and the development of the federal government.
whyRecommended: Provides a foundation in U.S. government and political institutions for students interested in public policy, law, campaigns, government relations, and political communication.

title: Animation and Motion Graphics
courseDescription: Provides hands-on experience designing and producing animation and motion graphics for digital, video, broadcast, and interactive media. Students develop visual concepts and turn them into polished animated media projects.
whyRecommended: Builds practical animation and visual-production skills for careers involving digital media, video, advertising, design, and visual storytelling.

title: Applied Music
courseDescription: Provides individualized instruction in a musical instrument or voice through weekly private lessons and independent practice. Students develop technique, musical interpretation, and performance ability under the guidance of an instructor.
whyRecommended: Provides sustained one-on-one performance training for students pursuing music, performance, composition, conducting, or other music-centered careers.

title: Foundations of Biology I
courseDescription: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life. Students study cell structure and function, DNA and genomes, metabolism, cellular energy, homeostasis, and how cells communicate and respond to their environment.
whyRecommended: Builds a foundation in cellular and molecular biology for students pursuing biology, health, laboratory science, biotechnology, and other life-science careers.
prerequisites: BL 151 must be taken previously or concurrently

title: Foundations of Biology I Lab
courseDescription: Introduces laboratory methods used in cellular and molecular biology. Students design experiments, use equipment such as microscopes and pipettes, collect and interpret data, perform scientific calculations, and communicate experimental results.
whyRecommended: Provides hands-on laboratory experience and develops the experimental skills needed for biology, healthcare, biotechnology, and scientific research.
prerequisites: BL 150 must be taken previously or concurrently

title: Biopsychology
courseDescription: Examines how biological processes influence behavior and mental activity. Students study the nervous system, brain function, neural communication, and the biological processes involved in emotion, behavior, and cognition.
whyRecommended: Connects psychology with neuroscience and biology for students interested in mental health, brain research, clinical psychology, neuropsychology, and behavioral science.

title: Business Intelligence and Data Mining
courseDescription: Introduces techniques for finding useful patterns and information in large business datasets. Students use business intelligence and data-mining tools to apply methods such as regression, clustering, and decision trees to real business problems.
whyRecommended: Builds practical analytics and data-mining skills for careers in data analytics, business intelligence, information systems, consulting, and other data-driven business fields.

title: Business Journalism
courseDescription: Teaches students how to report and explain stories involving businesses, financial markets, the economy, and corporate activity. Students learn to research business topics, interpret financial and economic information, interview sources, and communicate complex issues clearly to a general audience.
whyRecommended: Combines journalism, business, and economics for students interested in financial reporting, business media, corporate communications, and economic storytelling.

title: Business Statistics
courseDescription: Introduces statistical methods used to analyze business and economic data. Students learn descriptive statistics, statistical inference, hypothesis testing, regression, correlation, and methods for identifying trends in data.
whyRecommended: Builds quantitative analysis skills used throughout business, economics, finance, analytics, research, and data-driven decision-making.

title: Calculus I
courseDescription: Introduces the fundamental ideas of calculus, including limits, derivatives, differentiation techniques, antiderivatives, definite and indefinite integrals, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Students use these concepts to analyze how quantities change and solve mathematical problems.
whyRecommended: Develops mathematical reasoning and quantitative problem-solving skills used in mathematics, economics, data science, engineering, physics, finance, and other technical fields.
prerequisites: MA 109 or ALEKS score of 76 or higher or one year of high school calculus

title: Calculus II
courseDescription: Continues Calculus I with more advanced integration techniques and applications. Students also study improper integrals, parametric and polar equations, sequences, and infinite series.
whyRecommended: Develops advanced quantitative problem-solving skills used in mathematics, engineering, physics, computer science, data science, and other technical careers.
prerequisites: MA 251 with a grade of C- or better

title: Cell Biology
courseDescription: Examines how cells are structured and how they function at the molecular level. Students study cell organization, biochemical processes, communication between cells, and the mechanisms that control cellular activity.
whyRecommended: Provides advanced knowledge of cellular function for careers in biological research, biotechnology, medicine, pharmaceuticals, and related life sciences.

title: Child Development
courseDescription: Examines psychological development from infancy through childhood. Students study changes in thinking, language, emotions, personality, relationships, and behavior while comparing major theories of child development.
whyRecommended: Builds an understanding of children's behavior and development for careers in psychology, counseling, education, research, and youth services.

title: Childhood Psychopathology
courseDescription: Examines major psychological disorders that appear during childhood and adolescence. Students study how these disorders are identified, possible causes and developmental influences, and research on different approaches to treatment.
whyRecommended: Provides specialized knowledge of childhood mental health for students interested in clinical psychology, counseling, school psychology, and behavioral health.

title: Church and Empire: Early Medieval Art, c. 250-1050
courseDescription: Explores European art and architecture from the emergence of early Christian art through the medieval period. Students examine churches, mosaics, sculpture, manuscripts, reliquaries, and other works while studying how religion, political power, pilgrimage, and cultural change shaped medieval art.
whyRecommended: Develops art-historical and cultural analysis skills for students interested in museums, preservation, art history, historical research, and cultural institutions.

title: Cognitive Psychology
courseDescription: Examines how people process and use information. Students study memory, attention, problem solving, concept formation, conscious and unconscious thought, and connections between cognitive processes and the brain.
whyRecommended: Builds an understanding of human thinking and information processing for careers in psychology, user research, behavioral science, neuroscience, and human-centered technology.

title: Color Photography
courseDescription: Explores the technical and creative use of color in photography. Students create color photographs with digital cameras while studying color theory, the history of color photography, and how color affects the meaning and visual impact of an image.
whyRecommended: Strengthens technical photography and visual communication skills for careers in photography, digital media, visual storytelling, and creative production.

title: Communication Research
courseDescription: Introduces research methods used to study communication, media, advertising, public relations, journalism, and popular culture. Students learn how to design research, select appropriate methods, analyze data, and interpret research findings.
whyRecommended: Builds research and analytical skills for careers involving audience insights, advertising, media strategy, public relations, journalism, and social research.

title: Comprehensive Classroom Management
courseDescription: Examines practical approaches for managing classroom behavior and creating an effective learning environment. Students develop classroom rules, routines, behavior-management strategies, and intervention plans while considering how instruction, classroom structure, and student backgrounds affect behavior.
whyRecommended: Develops practical classroom-management and behavior-support skills for students preparing for teaching and education careers.

title: Computer-Aided Simulation and Design
courseDescription: Uses computer-based engineering tools to design and analyze mechanical parts and assemblies. Students create three-dimensional models, perform simulations such as finite-element analysis, and prepare detailed technical drawings and design documentation.
whyRecommended: Builds hands-on CAD, simulation, and engineering-design skills used in mechanical design, manufacturing, product development, and engineering analysis.

title: Consumer Behavior
courseDescription: Examines why consumers make purchasing decisions and how psychological, social, cultural, and demographic factors influence those decisions. Students learn to apply an understanding of consumer behavior when developing marketing strategies.
whyRecommended: Helps students understand how customers think and make decisions, which is useful in marketing, advertising, product development, branding, and market research.

title: Copy Editing
courseDescription: Develops the skills used to prepare written material for publication. Students edit and rewrite copy, correct errors, write headlines, proofread content, and improve the clarity and accuracy of news and other published writing.
whyRecommended: Builds professional editing and writing-quality skills for careers in journalism, publishing, communications, and digital media.

title: Costume Design
courseDescription: Introduces the process of designing costumes for theatrical productions. Students research historical and visual references, analyze scripts and characters, collaborate around a production concept, create costume renderings, and develop designs for plays from different periods and genres.
whyRecommended: Develops visual-design, research, and theatrical-production skills for students interested in costume design, theatre, fashion, and entertainment production.

title: Cyber Security and Digital Forensics
courseDescription: Introduces cybersecurity threats, vulnerabilities, privacy, security standards, and digital-forensics practices. Students examine how digital evidence is identified and analyzed while learning about the organizations, standards, and methods used to protect computer systems and investigate cyber incidents.
whyRecommended: Provides an accessible introduction to cybersecurity and digital investigations for students interested in forensic science, cybercrime, security, and technology.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
courseDescription: Studies equations used to model quantities that change over time. Students learn methods for solving and analyzing first- and second-order differential equations and systems of equations using analytical, numerical, and computer-based techniques.
whyRecommended: Develops mathematical modeling skills used throughout physics, engineering, applied mathematics, quantitative research, and other technical fields.
prerequisites: MA 351 or MA 252 with written permission of the instructor

title: Digital Logic and Computer Systems
courseDescription: Introduces the design of digital computer systems using logic gates, integrated circuits, registers, flip-flops, and other digital components. Students design combinational and sequential circuits and use state machines to understand how larger digital systems operate.
whyRecommended: Builds foundational digital-hardware design skills for students interested in computer engineering, electrical engineering, embedded systems, and computer hardware.

title: Digital Tools
courseDescription: Introduces digital tools used to create and publish media. Students develop practical experience with graphic design, image editing, web content, and other forms of digital media production.
whyRecommended: Builds practical digital-production skills used across advertising, journalism, graphic design, social media, and multimedia careers.

title: Directing I
courseDescription: Introduces the process of directing a theatrical performance. Students work through play selection, casting, rehearsals, staging, and coordination with costume, set, lighting, and sound design while directing scenes and short productions.
whyRecommended: Develops creative leadership, performance direction, and production-management skills for theatre and entertainment careers.

title: Discovering Information in Data
courseDescription: Teaches students how to acquire, clean, explore, analyze, and visualize real-world data. Students use Python-based tools to identify patterns, make data-driven decisions, and clearly communicate analytical results.
whyRecommended: Builds practical Python and data-analysis experience for careers in data science, analytics, research, technology, and other data-driven fields.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Discrete Structures
courseDescription: Introduces the mathematical ideas used to study computer science problems. Topics include logic, mathematical proofs, sets, functions, combinatorics, graphs, Boolean algebra, and recurrence relations.
whyRecommended: Builds the logical and mathematical foundation needed for algorithms, software engineering, theoretical computer science, and advanced data science.
prerequisites: MA 109 or higher, ALEKS score of 50 or higher, or one year of high school calculus

title: Dynamics
courseDescription: Studies the motion of particles and rigid bodies and the forces that cause that motion. Students solve engineering problems involving velocity, acceleration, forces, energy, momentum, and moving mechanical systems.
whyRecommended: Builds core mechanics skills used to analyze moving machines, vehicles, structures, and other mechanical systems.

title: Economics of Race and Inequality
courseDescription: Examines racial inequality and discrimination in the United States from an economic perspective. Students study disparities in employment, housing, education, and the criminal justice system and use economic research to evaluate potential policy solutions.
whyRecommended: Applies economic analysis to major social and policy issues for students interested in economics, public policy, social research, consulting, and community development.

title: Educational Psychology
courseDescription: Examines how psychological principles affect learning and teaching. Students study learning, motivation, memory, assessment, and other factors that influence how people learn in educational settings.
whyRecommended: Connects psychology with education and learning for careers involving teaching, student development, educational research, counseling, and psychology.

title: Electronics
courseDescription: Introduces the operation and design of electronic components and circuits. Students study operational amplifiers, diodes, transistors, MOSFETs, semiconductor behavior, amplifier circuits, and techniques used to analyze electronic systems.
whyRecommended: Builds fundamental electronics and circuit-design knowledge for careers involving electrical systems, computer hardware, embedded devices, and electronic engineering.

title: Electronics Lab
courseDescription: Provides hands-on laboratory experience with electronic components and circuits. Students test diodes and transistors, measure circuit behavior, build amplifier circuits, and compare experimental results with concepts learned in Electronics.
whyRecommended: Develops practical circuit-building, testing, and measurement skills for careers in electrical engineering, computer hardware, electronics, and embedded systems.

title: Encountering the Past
courseDescription: Introduces students to how historians study and interpret the past. Each section focuses on a different historical topic while teaching students to evaluate evidence, analyze primary and secondary sources, develop arguments, and connect historical events to issues in the present.
whyRecommended: Builds research, evidence analysis, and argumentative writing skills useful in history, law, policy, journalism, education, and other research-focused careers.

title: Engineering and Society: Engineering, Design, and Creative Problem Solving in the Built World
courseDescription: Explores engineering through the design of buildings, transportation systems, communication systems, and other parts of the built world. Students examine creative problem solving, visual design, and the social and historical effects of engineering decisions.
whyRecommended: Introduces engineering design and creative problem solving while helping students understand how engineering projects affect people and society.

title: Engineering Systems Analysis
courseDescription: Uses mathematical models to analyze and improve complex engineering systems. Students study system optimization, forecasting, reliability, decision analysis, economics, and how engineering choices affect a system throughout its life cycle.
whyRecommended: Develops systems-level analytical and decision-making skills for students interested in engineering design, optimization, operations, and technical leadership.

title: Effective Writing
courseDescription: Develops college-level writing through reading, research, drafting, revision, and editing. Students learn to create clear arguments, support ideas with evidence, adapt writing to different audiences, and improve their work through feedback.
whyRecommended: Strengthens professional writing, research, argumentation, and communication skills that are useful across nearly every academic and career field.

title: Environmental Biology
courseDescription: Introduces major environmental issues from a biological perspective. Students examine ecosystems, biodiversity, endangered species, climate change, habitat loss, conservation, and the ways human activity affects natural systems.
whyRecommended: Provides a biological foundation for understanding environmental problems and conservation for students interested in ecology, sustainability, environmental policy, and environmental science.

title: Environmental Ethics
courseDescription: Examines ethical questions about the relationship between humans and the natural world. Students consider responsibilities toward animals, ecosystems, natural resources, future generations, and the environmental consequences of personal and public decisions.
whyRecommended: Develops ethical reasoning for careers involving sustainability, environmental policy, conservation, corporate responsibility, and environmental decision-making.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
courseDescription: Examines the laws, regulations, and legal principles used to address environmental problems. Students study government regulation, pollution prevention, ecological restoration, and different legal and policy approaches to environmental protection.
whyRecommended: Builds knowledge of environmental regulation and policy for careers in sustainability, law, government, environmental consulting, and corporate compliance.

title: Environmental Science and Sustainability with Analysis
courseDescription: Studies natural environmental systems, human impacts, and sustainability using scientific and quantitative analysis. Students examine environmental conditions and use data to better understand issues involving ecosystems, pollution, resources, and human activity.
whyRecommended: Combines environmental science with quantitative analysis for students interested in sustainability, environmental research, policy, and environmental management.
prerequisites: CH 102 or CH 114 or BL 111 or BL 201
MA 109 or MA 151 or MA 251 or ST 110 or ST 210 or ST 265

title: Environmental Science and Sustainability
courseDescription: Examines environmental systems and sustainability through scientific investigation and data analysis. Students study how human activity affects natural systems and use environmental evidence to understand and evaluate real-world environmental problems.
whyRecommended: Develops scientific and analytical skills for careers involving environmental research, sustainability, conservation, and environmental problem-solving.

title: Experimental Methods
courseDescription: Introduces the design and execution of engineering experiments. Students collect and analyze measurements, evaluate experimental uncertainty, work with engineering sensors and data-acquisition methods, and communicate results through technical reports.
whyRecommended: Builds hands-on experimentation, measurement, and technical-analysis skills used across engineering careers.

title: Experimental Methods I & II
courseDescription: A two-course laboratory sequence focused on experimental methods used in modern physics. Students work with electronic instrumentation, experimental measurements, computer interfacing, and automated data collection.
whyRecommended: Provides advanced hands-on laboratory and instrumentation experience for students pursuing physics, scientific research, and experimental science careers.

title: Field Experience in Math Education
courseDescription: Provides supervised school-based experience connected to mathematics education. Students observe and work with learners in classroom settings while developing practical experience applying teaching methods to real students.
whyRecommended: Provides real classroom experience for students preparing to teach mathematics at the elementary level.

title: Financial Accounting
courseDescription: Introduces how businesses record financial activity and prepare financial statements for outside decision-makers. Students learn core accounting concepts, analyze business transactions, and use financial information to understand a company's performance and financial position.
whyRecommended: Builds practical accounting and Excel skills useful across accounting, finance, analytics, management, and other business careers.

title: Financial Management
courseDescription: Examines how companies make financial decisions about investing, financing, and managing their resources. Students study valuation, risk and return, financial markets, capital budgeting, cost of capital, and how businesses decide where to invest money.
whyRecommended: Builds corporate finance and financial decision-making skills used across finance, accounting, business analysis, consulting, and management careers.

title: Intermediate German II
courseDescription: Completes Loyola's intermediate German sequence by reinforcing and expanding speaking, listening, reading, and writing while deepening cultural awareness. The course serves as the Intermediate II capstone, with students generally working toward ACTFL intermediate-mid proficiency.
whyRecommended: Builds practical German communication and cultural competence useful for study abroad and internationally oriented work.
prerequisites: GR 103 or appropriate placement into GR 104

title: Global Environment
courseDescription: Introduces Earth as an interconnected system and examines how human activity affects climate, biodiversity, pollution, water availability, and planetary boundaries. Students use systems thinking and connect environmental problems with questions of environmental justice.
whyRecommended: Builds a systems-level foundation for understanding environmental problems that is useful in science, sustainability, conservation, and policy work.

title: Global Environment of Business
courseDescription: Examines the social, political, economic, cultural, and legal environments that shape cross-border business. Students analyze cultural differences, globalization risks and opportunities, and the interests of businesses, institutions, policymakers, and other global stakeholders.
whyRecommended: Helps students evaluate the external forces that shape international business decisions, markets, and stakeholder relationships.

title: Global Environmental Politics
courseDescription: Examines why international cooperation on climate change is difficult through environmental theory, public policy, and activism. Students complete substantial readings and an independent project with an activism component, with Indigenous and Native peoples' experiences centered in the course.
whyRecommended: Develops policy and advocacy skills for students interested in climate governance, environmental justice, and public-sector sustainability work.

title: Global Media & Journalism
courseDescription: Explores journalism and media in an international context, focusing on how news and media operate across national and cultural boundaries. Students examine global journalism through a cross-cultural lens and consider how international contexts shape media practice.
whyRecommended: Builds a global perspective on journalism that is useful for reporting, producing, and media-analysis roles involving international audiences or issues.

title: Graphics I
department: Visual & Performing Arts / Communication and Media
courseDescription: Introduces core digital graphics workflows, including file formats, bitmap image editing, vector drawing, and page layout. Students build practical experience with industry-standard graphics software for visual journalism, design, and media production.
whyRecommended: Provides hands-on visual design skills that transfer directly to graphic design, digital media, publishing, and visual journalism work.

title: Heat and Mass Transfer
courseDescription: Examines heat and mass transfer in engineering systems, including steady and transient conduction, internal and external convection, radiation, and heat exchangers. Students also study relationships between heat and mass transport and apply them to thermal-system analysis and design.
whyRecommended: Builds core thermal-system analysis skills used in mechanical design, HVAC, energy systems, and other heat-transfer-intensive engineering work.

title: Our Rights: A History of Civil and Human Rights Law in America
courseDescription: Examines the development of civil and human rights law in the United States and the social, political, and economic forces that shaped it. Students analyze important legal decisions, Supreme Court opinions, and recurring debates over rights and equality in American society.
whyRecommended: Develops historical and legal analysis skills useful for careers involving law, public policy, civil rights, advocacy, and government.

title: Human Neuropsychology
courseDescription: Examines relationships between brain structures and human cognition and behavior. Students study basic neuroanatomy, functions of different regions of the cerebral cortex, and the cognitive and behavioral effects of neurological disorders.
whyRecommended: Provides a strong brain-behavior foundation for students interested in neuropsychology, clinical psychology, neuroscience research, or rehabilitation.

title: Industrial/Organizational Psychology
courseDescription: Applies psychological principles to people and behavior in workplace settings. Students examine individual and group behavior within organizations and topics such as employee recruitment, selection, performance evaluation, and organizational functioning.
whyRecommended: Connects psychology directly to workplace decision-making and is especially useful for careers in human resources, talent management, and organizational consulting.

title: Marketing Communications
courseDescription: Examines how organizations coordinate promotional communication across channels to support their marketing strategy. Students study areas such as advertising, media planning, digital marketing, sales promotion, public relations, and the planning of integrated marketing communication programs.
whyRecommended: Builds practical skills for planning coordinated brand and promotional campaigns across advertising, digital, public relations, and other marketing channels.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
courseDescription: Studies the economy-wide forces that drive long-term growth and short-term fluctuations. Students analyze national income, unemployment, business cycles, international trade and finance, monetary and fiscal policy, economic growth, expectations, and policy credibility.
whyRecommended: Builds the macroeconomic modeling and policy-analysis foundation needed for economics, finance, forecasting, consulting, and public-policy work.
prerequisites: EC 102, EC 103, and either MA 151 or MA 251

title: International Business Law
courseDescription: Examines the laws and legal systems that affect companies operating across national borders. Students study international sales contracts, dispute resolution, trade regulation, intellectual property, import and export rules, and host-country regulations affecting business.
whyRecommended: Builds the legal and regulatory awareness needed to evaluate international transactions, compliance risks, and cross-border business decisions.

title: International Communication
courseDescription: Examines communication from an international perspective and develops students' understanding of communication across national and cultural contexts. Students analyze global communication issues and how media and communication operate within an increasingly interconnected world.
whyRecommended: Develops a global perspective on media and communication useful for international advertising, public relations, journalism, and communications work.

title: Interpersonal Behavior
courseDescription: Examines psychological concepts involved in communication, motivation, and interpersonal learning. Students explore how these processes operate in friendships, intimate relationships, parenting, marriage, and workplace relationships.
whyRecommended: Helps students understand and evaluate interpersonal relationships, making it useful for counseling, human resources, organizational development, and other people-focused careers.

title: Introduction to Book Publishing
courseDescription: Introduces the book publishing industry from the publisher's perspective. Students examine editorial management, promotion, design, production, and other processes involved in bringing books from manuscripts to published products.
whyRecommended: Provides a practical overview of the publishing process for students interested in editorial, publishing, media, or book-marketing careers.

title: Introduction to Counseling
courseDescription: Introduces the basic principles, theories, techniques, and professional practices of counseling and psychotherapy. Students examine major counseling approaches and develop an understanding of what occurs during the counseling process.
whyRecommended: Provides an early foundation in counseling theory and practice for students considering clinical psychology, counseling, social services, or related helping professions.

title: Introduction to Education: School and Society
courseDescription: Examines education in a multicultural society through historical and sociological perspectives, theories of how children learn, student achievement, and educational technology. Students also gain hands-on experience working with K-12 pupils through a concurrent school-based field experience.
whyRecommended: Gives prospective educators an early combination of educational theory and direct school experience before they move into advanced teaching coursework.
prerequisites: Closed to students who have taken ED 101

title: Introduction to Engineering
courseDescription: Introduces engineering as both a profession and a problem-solving discipline. Students practice design, creative problem solving, innovation, teamwork, and consideration of how engineering solutions affect society.
whyRecommended: Provides an early hands-on foundation in engineering design and teamwork before students move into more specialized engineering coursework.

title: Introduction to Forensic Science with Lab
courseDescription: Introduces forensic science and the use of scientific evidence in legal investigations. Students study areas such as crime-scene investigation, DNA analysis, questioned documents, forensic psychology, and toxicology while gaining laboratory experience with evidence-analysis techniques.
whyRecommended: Provides foundational laboratory and investigative experience for students pursuing forensic science, crime-scene, or forensic laboratory careers.
prerequisites: Restricted to Forensic Science majors or minors, or written permission of the department chair

title: Introduction to Integral Ecology
courseDescription: Examines integral ecology as an interdisciplinary approach to understanding how people can care justly for Earth and its interconnected human and natural systems. Students explore environmental questions through perspectives including literature, philosophy, theology, history, and the arts.
whyRecommended: Builds interdisciplinary environmental reasoning useful for sustainability, environmental policy, advocacy, and community-focused environmental work.

title: Computer Science through Programming
courseDescription: Introduces computer science through problem solving and programming in Python. Students break complex problems into smaller steps, work with numeric and textual data, use conditionals, loops, and basic data structures, test their solutions, and explore broader areas of computing.
whyRecommended: Provides a rigorous first programming foundation for students pursuing software, data science, quantitative, or other computation-heavy careers.

title: Introductory Psychology
courseDescription: Surveys psychology as both a science and a profession. Students examine biological, cognitive, and social influences on behavior and mental processes while learning how psychological research and critical thinking are used to evaluate questions about human behavior.
whyRecommended: Provides the foundational knowledge of human behavior and psychological research needed for later psychology coursework and many health, research, and people-focused careers.

title: Introduction to Public History
courseDescription: Explores how history is interpreted and presented in public settings, with particular attention to historical sites in Baltimore and elsewhere in the United States. Students apply public-history concepts by developing a proposal for their own public history project.
whyRecommended: Connects historical research with public-facing work in museums, historic sites, preservation, archives, and cultural organizations.

title: Introduction to Programming in Python
courseDescription: Introduces software development and programming in Python with an emphasis on real-world applications. Students practice program design, programming structures, data structures, testing, and debugging while applying programming to analytical and business problems.
whyRecommended: Builds practical Python programming skills for students interested in business analytics, information systems, data-focused roles, and technology-enabled decision making.

title: Introduction to Sociology
courseDescription: Introduces the foundations of sociology and the systematic study of society. Students examine major sociological theories, methods of social inquiry, social order and change, and how larger social structures influence individuals and groups.
whyRecommended: Develops a structured way to analyze social institutions, inequality, communities, and human behavior that is useful in research, policy, advocacy, and social-service careers.

title: Introduction to Theatre Design
courseDescription: Introduces the fundamental principles of scenic, costume, and lighting design for theatre. Students develop design vocabulary, practice collaborating with others, apply design principles to scripts and theatrical spaces, and complete projects in all three design areas.
whyRecommended: Provides hands-on foundations across the major theatrical design disciplines for students interested in theatre production, entertainment design, and technical arts careers.

title: Introduction to Linux
courseDescription: Provides a lab-based introduction to fundamental Linux and UNIX operating-system concepts. Students develop practical familiarity with working in a Linux environment and the tools used throughout computer science coursework.
whyRecommended: Builds practical operating-system and command-line experience useful for software development, systems administration, cybersecurity, and technical computing.

title: Law and Social Justice
courseDescription: Examines controversial contemporary issues at the intersection of law and social justice, including topics such as voting rights, immigration, discrimination, disability rights, and mass incarceration. Students use debates and interactive exercises to evaluate competing arguments and consider how law shapes social outcomes.
whyRecommended: Develops legal reasoning and structured argumentation for students interested in law, advocacy, public policy, and social-impact careers.

title: Law in Literature
courseDescription: Explores enduring legal and ethical questions through literary works and their cultural contexts. Students analyze how literature represents ideas about justice, law, responsibility, authority, and conflicts between individuals and society.
whyRecommended: Strengthens close reading, argumentation, and ethical reasoning for students considering law, policy, writing, or other analysis-intensive careers.

title: Introduction to Linear Algebra
courseDescription: Introduces matrices, linear transformations, vector spaces, linear independence, systems of equations, eigenvalues, and diagonalization. Students also apply linear algebra to problems such as computer graphics, least-squares analysis, and economic input-output models while using MATLAB.
whyRecommended: Provides core mathematical tools used throughout data science, quantitative economics, scientific computing, modeling, and advanced mathematics.

title: Linear Circuit Analysis
courseDescription: Introduces systematic techniques for analyzing linear electrical circuits using element models, Kirchhoff's laws, mesh and node equations, superposition, and Thévenin and Norton equivalents. Students also examine transient responses, energy-storage circuits, sinusoidal steady-state behavior, and phasor analysis.
whyRecommended: Builds the circuit-analysis foundation needed for electronics, computer hardware, electrical systems, and later engineering design courses.

title: Location Analytics
courseDescription: Examines how organizations analyze geographically referenced data such as ZIP codes and latitude-longitude coordinates to support business decisions. Students use GeoDa and spatial-analysis techniques for applications such as logistics, market analysis, and real estate management.
whyRecommended: Adds spatial analysis to a student's analytics toolkit for careers involving geographic data, business intelligence, markets, logistics, or real estate.

title: Macroeconomic Principles
courseDescription: Introduces economy-wide topics including GDP, unemployment, inflation, business cycles, money and banking, national debt, and aggregate demand and supply. Students also examine fiscal and monetary policy, international trade, foreign exchange markets, and how policy changes affect economic outcomes.
whyRecommended: Builds the economic foundation needed to understand markets, government policy, business cycles, and the broader forces affecting firms and financial decisions.

title: Managerial Accounting
courseDescription: Introduces accounting information used by managers for internal planning and decision-making. Students study manufacturing costs, job-order costing, incremental analysis, standard costs, budgeting, and cash-flow information.
whyRecommended: Develops the cost-analysis and budgeting skills used in accounting, finance, management, consulting, and business decision-making.

title: Managing Stress and Tension
courseDescription: Examines psychological approaches to understanding and managing stress and tension. Students explore stress responses, coping strategies, and ways psychological concepts can be applied to managing stress in everyday life.
whyRecommended: Provides applied knowledge of stress and coping that is useful in counseling, clinical psychology, health psychology, wellness, and other helping professions.

title: Marketing
courseDescription: Introduces how organizations create value for customers through marketing. Students study market research, consumer behavior, segmentation, targeting, positioning, and decisions involving products, promotion, pricing, and distribution.
whyRecommended: Provides the foundational marketing concepts needed for careers involving customers, brands, sales, product strategy, and business growth.

title: Mathematics of Sustainability
courseDescription: Uses quantitative reasoning to evaluate sustainability questions and construct evidence-based arguments. Students examine measurement, flows, connectivity, change, risk, decision-making, and mathematical models of sustainability at local, regional, and global scales.
whyRecommended: Builds quantitative modeling and risk-analysis skills for students interested in sustainability, environmental economics, climate risk, and evidence-based environmental decision-making.
prerequisites: Closed to students who have credit for MA/ST 200-level courses

title: Mechanical Design
courseDescription: Applies mechanics of materials and other engineering principles to the design of mechanical components. Students analyze deflection, failure criteria, reliability, fatigue, shafts, bearings, gears, belts, springs, fasteners, and related machine elements.
whyRecommended: Develops the applied engineering-design and failure-analysis skills used to create reliable mechanical products and components.

title: Media and the Political Process
courseDescription: Examines how journalism, advertising, public relations, and other forms of media interact with the American political system. Students analyze scholarly and popular media research and write about current political issues and events.
whyRecommended: Develops media-analysis, research, and political communication skills useful for journalism, campaigns, public affairs, and political communications.

title: Integrated Science I / Integrated Science II
courseDescription: Forms a two-course interdisciplinary science sequence designed specifically for Elementary Education majors. Students explore connected concepts from physics, chemistry, biology, Earth science, and astronomy through activity-based and inquiry-oriented scientific work.
whyRecommended: Builds the broad scientific understanding and hands-on investigation skills elementary educators need to teach science across multiple disciplines.
prerequisites: PH 116: Restricted to Elementary Education majors; no course prerequisite
PH 117: PH 116; restricted to Elementary Education majors

title: History Seminar
courseDescription: Represents Loyola's rotating series of advanced history seminars, each focused intensively on a specific historical topic. Students engage deeply with primary and secondary sources, participate in discussion, evaluate historical arguments, and complete substantial research and writing.
whyRecommended: Provides advanced research and writing experience for students pursuing historical research, archives, museums, policy, or other research-intensive careers.
prerequisites: Written permission of the instructor is required for current seminar offerings; additional prerequisites depend on the specific HS 460-498 seminar

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology I / II
courseDescription: Forms Loyola's two-course human anatomy and physiology sequence for students pursuing nursing, allied health, and biological study. Students examine how human body structures support physiological functions across systems including muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urinary, immune, and reproductive systems, with required laboratory work reinforcing lecture material.
whyRecommended: Provides detailed knowledge of human body systems and laboratory experience foundational to nursing, health professions, and organismal biology.
prerequisites: BL 206: BL 118, BL 119, BL 121, and BL 126; or BL 150, BL 151, BL 152, and BL 153; or equivalent; BL 207 must be taken concurrently
BL 208: BL 206 and BL 207; BL 209 must be taken concurrently
Written or electronic permission of the department chair or director of curriculum and advising
BL 206 and BL 208 are closed to students who have taken BL 260, BL 301, or BL 452

title: Introductory and Intermediate German
courseDescription: Represents Loyola's four-course introductory and intermediate German language sequence, culminating in GR 104. Students progressively develop German speaking, listening, reading, and writing while building knowledge of German-speaking cultures and literature.
whyRecommended: Builds practical German proficiency and intercultural knowledge useful for international affairs, translation, diplomacy, and cross-cultural professional work.
prerequisites: Placement determines the appropriate entry point in the GR 101-104 sequence
GR 101: Intended for students beginning German
GR 103: Completion of the introductory German sequence or appropriate placement

title: Media, Culture, and Society
courseDescription: Examines how media shape culture, social life, and the way people understand the world around them. Students analyze media and cultural products such as television, music, books, and advertising to identify the social meanings they communicate and the effects media can have on society.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in understanding how media influence audiences, culture, public attitudes, and the broader social environment surrounding communication.

title: Media Ethics
courseDescription: Examines ethical issues and principles that shape contemporary communication and media. Students evaluate professional media decisions and consider questions involving truth, fairness, responsibility, competing interests, and the effects communication choices can have on audiences and the public.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students entering journalism, advertising, public relations, or other media careers where they will need to evaluate the ethical consequences of professional communication decisions.

title: Media Writing
courseDescription: Builds foundational story-writing skills that can be used across journalism, digital media, public relations, and advertising. Students learn to gather information, organize clear media stories, and adapt their writing to different professional communication formats and audiences.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want a strong foundation in concise, audience-focused professional writing that transfers across journalism, advertising, public relations, and digital communication.

title: Microbiology Lab
courseDescription: Develops hands-on microbiology skills including sterile cultivation of microorganisms, staining procedures, selective and differential media, diagnostic tests, and antibiotic-sensitivity testing. Students apply these laboratory methods to identify unknown microbial cultures.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students pursuing biological, clinical, nursing, biotechnology, or laboratory careers that require practical experience culturing, testing, and identifying microorganisms.

title: Microeconomic Principles
courseDescription: Introduces how consumers, businesses, and markets make decisions about what is produced, how it is produced, and who receives it. Students use supply and demand, production and cost concepts, and different market structures to analyze pricing, firm behavior, labor and capital markets, inequality, environmental issues, and other economic choices.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to understand how markets, consumers, and firms make decisions and to build the economic reasoning used in business, finance, policy, consulting, and market analysis.

title: Music Fundamentals
courseDescription: Introduces the basic systems that organize music, including acoustics, rhythm, melody, harmony, tonality, and musical form. Students connect these concepts through listening, reading music, writing musical material, and performing.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want a practical foundation in how music is structured and represented before moving into theory, musicianship, composition, or advanced performance study.

title: Music History I: Medieval to Baroque
courseDescription: Surveys Western art music from the Medieval period through the Baroque era, roughly 500 to 1750. Students study Gregorian chant, early musical notation, polyphony, Renaissance music, opera, cantatas, and concertos through listening, score study, and historical readings while connecting musical styles to the religious, political, and cultural settings in which they developed.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to understand how Western musical styles developed and strengthen their ability to connect musical works with their historical and cultural contexts.
prerequisites: MU 201 or MU 302; either may be taken previously or concurrently

title: Musicianship I
courseDescription: Develops practical ear-training and sight-singing abilities so students can recognize, reproduce, and write down musical material accurately. Students practice melodic and harmonic intervals, rhythms, complete melodies, chord qualities, and harmonic progressions through performance and aural dictation.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want stronger musical ears, more accurate sight-reading, and the ability to recognize and reproduce musical patterns without relying only on written notation.
prerequisites: MU 201 must be taken previously or concurrently

title: News Reporting and Writing
courseDescription: Provides hands-on practice in reporting and writing the basic news stories expected of entry-level journalists for print and online publication. Students develop interviewing and story-research techniques while practicing professional standards including verification, objectivity, fairness, and balance.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want practical reporting experience and the research, interviewing, verification, and news-writing skills used in professional journalism.

title: Nursing Care of Adults and Older Adults 1 & 2
courseDescription: Develops nursing care for adults and older adults across preventive care, acute illness, chronic disease, and hospice or palliative settings. Students apply clinical judgment and the nursing process while studying acute and chronic conditions, aging, patient education, documentation, ethics, cultural needs, therapeutic care, and safety.
whyRecommended: Recommended for nursing students preparing to care for adult and older-adult patients while developing the clinical judgment used in medical-surgical and geriatric nursing.
prerequisites: Completion of nursing prerequisite courses; NUR 210, NUR 211, NUR 215, and NUR 216

title: Nursing Professional Development in Clinical Judgment Seminar
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment by introducing evidence-based practice, the nursing process, clinical reasoning, patient-safety concepts, and risk reduction. Students also examine health-information privacy, professional ethics, and communication within multidisciplinary and interprofessional healthcare teams.
whyRecommended: Recommended for nursing students building the reasoning, evidence-based decision-making, and professional communication skills needed before entering more advanced clinical coursework.

title: Nursing Professional Development in Catholic Tradition Seminar
courseDescription: Introduces nursing professionalism through Loyola's Jesuit and Catholic tradition, including reflective self-awareness, discernment, care of the whole person, equity, and social justice. Students also examine the history of professional nursing, healthcare delivery systems, Catholic healthcare, and social determinants of health in Baltimore.
whyRecommended: Recommended for nursing students beginning their professional formation and learning how ethics, reflection, social context, and whole-person care shape nursing practice.

title: Object-Oriented Engineering Design
courseDescription: Applies object-oriented programming and design to computer engineering problems. Students work with topics including TCP/IP communication, interprocess communication, graphical user interfaces, database interfaces, and engineering design practices.
whyRecommended: Recommended for engineering students who want to connect software design with communications, interfaces, databases, and computer-controlled engineering systems.

title: Object-Oriented Software Design
courseDescription: Builds object-oriented software design and data-structure skills using Java. Students practice object-oriented analysis and design, inheritance and interfaces, generics, the Java Collections Framework, testing and debugging, recursion, trees, maps and sets, and advanced sorting algorithms.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want stronger software-development foundations and experience designing larger programs with reusable object-oriented structures and advanced data structures.

title: Supply Chain and Operations Management
courseDescription: Examines how organizations design and operate systems that transform resources into goods and services. Students study operations strategy, process design, product and process quality, productivity, global supply chains, environmental impacts, and qualitative and quantitative methods for improving operational decisions.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in improving how organizations produce goods, deliver services, manage supply chains, and make operational decisions.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 must be taken concurrently

title: Organic Chemistry I
courseDescription: Introduces the language, theory, and problem-solving methods of organic chemistry. Students study acid-base chemistry, molecular conformations, stereochemistry, reactions of aliphatic compounds, organic synthesis, and reaction mechanisms, with emphasis on applications to biology and medicine.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students pursuing chemistry, biology, biochemistry, medicine, or related laboratory sciences who need to understand organic molecular structures, reactions, and synthesis.

title: Organic Chemistry Lab I
courseDescription: Provides hands-on experience with the laboratory methods used to work with organic compounds. Students practice techniques for isolating, purifying, and synthesizing organic substances while applying concepts from Organic Chemistry I.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who need practical experience carrying out organic chemistry procedures and preparing, isolating, and purifying compounds in the laboratory.

title: Introductory Physics I with Lab
courseDescription: Introduces classical physics without requiring calculus, covering mechanics, fluids, heat, and thermodynamics. The integrated laboratory develops experimental measurement, error analysis, data interpretation, and scientific report-writing skills.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students in the life sciences who need a practical foundation in mechanics, energy, fluids, and thermal physics together with hands-on laboratory experience.

title: General Physics Lab I
courseDescription: Introduces experimental physics through mechanics-based laboratory work. Students learn precise measurement, treatment and presentation of experimental data, uncertainty and error analysis, and the comparison of experimental results with physical models.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who need hands-on experience collecting and evaluating physical measurements while learning the experimental methods used in physics, chemistry, and engineering.

title: Politics
courseDescription: Introduces the basic principles and problems studied in political science. Students examine the origins, powers, and limits of the state and analyze how political authority, institutions, and political processes shape collective decisions.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in government, public policy, law, or political research who want a foundation for analyzing political institutions and decision-making.

title: Probability and Statistics
courseDescription: Develops probability and statistical methods for analyzing uncertain events and numerical data. Students study random experiments and variables, probability distributions, expected values, descriptive statistics, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and simple linear regression.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students in engineering, quantitative science, or forensic work who need probability models and statistical methods for analyzing data and making evidence-based decisions.

title: Professional Writing
courseDescription: Develops clear, reader-centered writing for professional settings and different workplace audiences. Students create practical documents such as résumés, cover letters, memos, reports, and proposals while conducting research and adapting their writing to the expectations of their field.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want practical experience producing the workplace documents used in job searches, professional communication, research, and organizational decision-making.

title: Programming Languages
courseDescription: Examines major programming-language concepts and different approaches to structuring programs, including imperative, functional, logic, and object-oriented paradigms. Students compare how languages behave and learn principles for understanding, evaluating, and adapting to unfamiliar programming languages.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to move beyond individual programming languages and understand the deeper concepts that make it easier to learn, compare, and choose languages for different software problems.

title: Programming Tools for Engineering and Science
courseDescription: Introduces programming fundamentals for solving engineering and scientific problems, including data types, conditionals, loops, procedural decomposition, and basic data structures. Students also learn introductory software design and testing concepts and explore applications within computer engineering.
whyRecommended: Recommended for engineering students who need a programming foundation for computational problem solving, software testing, and later engineering design courses.

title: Project Management
courseDescription: Develops the methods used to plan, execute, monitor, control, and complete projects successfully. Students examine the full project life cycle, use project-management tools and technology, and consider the organizational and human challenges created by change and project implementation.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in managing complex projects, coordinating teams and resources, and keeping business initiatives on schedule and aligned with organizational goals.

title: Psychopathology
courseDescription: Examines psychological disorders and the ways abnormal patterns of behavior, thought, and emotion are defined and classified. Students study explanations for how disorders develop, research findings on different forms of psychopathology, and cultural and ethical issues involved in understanding mental disorders.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in clinical psychology, counseling, mental health, or forensic work who want to understand the characteristics and development of psychological disorders.

title: Public Speaking
courseDescription: Develops the ability to research, organize, and deliver effective oral presentations for different audiences and purposes. Students practice informative and persuasive speaking, individual and collaborative presentations, delivery techniques, and constructive evaluation of speeches.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want stronger presentation, persuasion, and audience-communication skills for careers that require explaining ideas clearly and speaking confidently in professional settings.

title: Quantitative Chemical Analysis
courseDescription: Introduces analytical chemistry with an emphasis on chemical equilibria, quantitative measurements, and evaluating experimental data and error. Students study gravimetric, volumetric, and potentiometric analysis while building a foundation for later work in physical chemistry, instrumental analysis, and laboratory methods.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want a rigorous foundation in measuring chemical composition, interpreting quantitative laboratory data, and applying analytical methods used in chemistry and forensic laboratories.

title: Real Estate
courseDescription: Examines the development of unimproved land and the rehabilitation of existing properties across office, retail, residential, mixed-use, and specialized real estate projects. Students study market analysis, site acquisition, due diligence, zoning, approvals, site planning, construction, financing, leasing, sustainability, property management, and disposition.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in real estate development who want to understand how properties move from market analysis and site acquisition through financing, construction, leasing, and eventual disposition.

title: Real Estate Finance and Investment
courseDescription: Examines how real estate value is established and how financial principles are applied to property investments. Students analyze time value of money, return on investment, net operating income, sources and uses of funds, debt and equity financing, investment returns, sensitivity analysis, risk, and exit strategies.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in real estate investing, acquisitions, development, or finance who want to evaluate property value, financing structures, investment returns, and risk.

title: Real Estate Modeling and Valuation
courseDescription: Develops advanced financial modeling and valuation skills for the development or acquisition of office, multifamily, hotel, and residential properties. Students build real estate models involving debt schedules, alternative financing structures, joint-venture waterfalls, return allocations, REIT concepts, and sustainability considerations.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students pursuing real estate investment or development who want hands-on experience evaluating property cash flows, financing structures, returns, and investment value.

title: Recording Studio I
courseDescription: Provides hands-on experience recording music and speech in Loyola's recording studio using live and studio multitrack techniques. Students learn recording equipment, audio editing methods, software applications, and the technical and creative principles used to produce recorded sound.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in music production, audio engineering, broadcasting, or digital media who want practical experience recording and editing professional-quality audio.

title: Research Methods I (with Lab)
courseDescription: Introduces the full psychological research process, beginning with forming research questions and reviewing scientific literature. Students work with research designs, questionnaires and surveys, basic statistical techniques, data collection, and the methods needed to develop and document their own studies.
whyRecommended: Recommended for psychology students who want hands-on experience designing studies and working with the research methods used in behavioral science, clinical research, and graduate-level psychology.

title: Scene Design
courseDescription: Develops theatrical scene-design skills through projects based on productions from different styles and historical periods. Students research visual concepts and create designer elevations, ground plans, drawings, and models while learning how scenic designers collaborate with directors.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in theatrical design or production who want practical experience turning scripts and production concepts into workable scenic environments.

title: Selling Concepts and Strategies
courseDescription: Develops customer-focused selling skills using a needs-based approach to products, services, and ideas. Students practice prospecting, sales planning, relationship management, adaptive selling, persuasive communication, active listening, and identifying customer needs.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in sales, marketing, business development, or client-facing work who want practical experience building customer relationships and communicating value persuasively.

title: Signals and Systems
courseDescription: Introduces the mathematical tools used to represent and analyze continuous-time and discrete-time signals and systems. Students work with convolution, Fourier series and transforms, Laplace transforms, sampling, difference equations, frequency-domain representations, and the z-transform.
whyRecommended: Recommended for computer and electrical engineering students preparing for advanced work in signal processing, communications, controls, electronics, and other systems-based engineering fields.

title: Social Media for Social Justice
courseDescription: Examines how social media and digital communication intersect with social justice, race, inequality, and public advocacy. Students critically analyze how online platforms shape discussion of social issues and how digital media can be used to communicate about justice and social change.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in media, advocacy, nonprofit communication, or public relations who want to understand how social platforms influence social-justice conversations and public engagement.

title: Social Power and Social Change
courseDescription: Examines how institutions such as the state, economy, and society organize and distribute power and how those institutions change over time. Students use comparative, historical, and sociological perspectives to analyze large-scale patterns of social organization and transformation.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in sociology, policy, global affairs, or social research who want to understand how institutions and power relationships shape major social changes.

title: Social Psychology
courseDescription: Examines how other people and social situations influence thoughts, feelings, and behavior. Students study topics such as attitudes and persuasion, prejudice, attribution, interpersonal attraction, helping, aggression, conformity, and group influence.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in understanding how social environments shape behavior, relationships, attitudes, and decision-making.

title: Software Engineering
courseDescription: Covers the practices used to develop larger software systems from planning through implementation and testing. Students work with requirements, software design, development processes, testing strategies, documentation, and collaborative software development through a substantial team project.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students preparing for professional software development who want experience building, testing, and documenting larger systems as part of a development team.

title: Solid Mechanics
courseDescription: Examines how solid materials and structural components deform and carry loads. Students analyze stress and strain, axial loading, torsion, bending, shear, combined loading, stress transformations, and the behavior of beams and shafts.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students pursuing mechanical, materials, or related engineering work that requires predicting how components respond to forces and designing structures that resist failure.

title: Intermediate Spanish II
courseDescription: Continues Intermediate Spanish I by strengthening speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills while expanding students' vocabulary and grammatical control. Students also deepen their understanding of Spanish-speaking cultures and work toward greater independence communicating in Spanish.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want stronger practical Spanish proficiency and preparation for advanced conversation, composition, literature, and culture courses.

title: Special Topics in Art History
courseDescription: Provides an intensive investigation of a changing art-historical topic, which may focus on a particular artist, period, issue, or artistic problem. Students combine close study of artworks with historical research, discussion, and seminar-style analysis, with the exact subject changing by semester.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want advanced, focused study of a specific art-historical subject while strengthening visual analysis and research skills.

title: Special Topics in Clinical, Counseling, and Health Psychology
courseDescription: Provides advanced study of a selected issue in clinical, counseling, or health psychology, with the specific subject changing by offering. Students examine current psychological theory and research related to the semester's topic and apply evidence to questions involving mental or behavioral health.
whyRecommended: Recommended for psychology students who want advanced exposure to a focused clinical, counseling, or health psychology topic before graduate study or behavioral-health work.

title: Special Topics in Communication
courseDescription: Provides upper-level study of a specialized communication or media subject that changes from one offering to another. Students investigate the selected topic through communication analysis, research, discussion, and course-specific projects or assignments.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to explore an emerging or specialized area of communication and media beyond Loyola's regularly scheduled courses.

title: Sports Writing
courseDescription: Develops reporting and storytelling skills for covering sports across several journalistic formats. Students practice traditional game coverage as well as features, opinion pieces, essays, and more narrative approaches to sports journalism.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in sports media who want practical experience reporting events, developing sports stories, and writing for journalistic audiences.

title: Stagecraft
courseDescription: Introduces the practical backstage work required to produce live theatre through supervised, hands-on experience. Students work in areas such as set construction, scene painting, stage lighting, and production crews while contributing to Loyola theatre productions.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in theatre production who want practical experience building scenery, working with lighting, and supporting live performances backstage.

title: Statics
courseDescription: Examines the mechanics of rigid bodies that are at rest or moving at constant velocity. Students work with force vectors, particle and rigid-body equilibrium, structural analysis, internal forces, friction, centroids, centers of gravity, and moments of inertia.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students preparing for engineering or applied-physics work that requires analyzing forces, loads, and the equilibrium of structures and mechanical systems.

title: Introduction to Statistics
courseDescription: Introduces statistical analysis without requiring calculus. Students learn descriptive statistics, regression, probability, normal and binomial distributions, sampling distributions, estimation, and hypothesis testing.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who need a practical foundation in analyzing data, evaluating uncertainty, testing claims, and interpreting quantitative evidence across research and professional settings.
prerequisites: MA 109 or a score of 65 or higher on ALEKS or one year of high school calculus

title: Statistics for Decision Making
courseDescription: A current Loyola University Maryland undergraduate course with this exact title or a documented current equivalent could not be verified. Loyola currently offers ST 110, ST 210, and EC 220 as distinct introductory statistics courses, so assigning this ID to one of them without evidence could create an incorrect duplicate.
whyRecommended: This entry should not be recommended until the intended Loyola course is confirmed.

title: Strategic Management
courseDescription: Examines how organizations establish direction and make executive-level decisions that create and sustain competitive advantage. Students analyze internal and external environments and practice formulating, implementing, and evaluating strategic plans while integrating knowledge from different business functions.
