whyRecommended: Recommended for students preparing for management, consulting, or strategy roles where they must evaluate organizations, identify competitive challenges, and develop coordinated plans for long-term performance.

title: Structure of Music: Theory I
courseDescription: Studies melodic and harmonic practices common in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century music. Students build music-theory skills through written exercises, analysis, ear training, sight-singing, and other activities that connect written theory with hearing and performing music.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students pursuing advanced music study who want stronger foundations in harmony, musical analysis, ear training, and sight-singing.

title: Survey of Finance
courseDescription: Introduces students to the financial services industry and the range of career opportunities and professional pathways available within finance. Students develop a broad understanding of the field before choosing more specialized coursework or career directions.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students exploring finance who want an overview of the industry, its major professional areas, and the different career paths available before taking advanced finance courses.

title: Information Systems Analysis and Design
courseDescription: Examines how information systems are planned, analyzed, designed, and implemented to meet organizational needs. Students use Agile and design-thinking approaches to identify user requirements, develop user stories and prototypes, work through development sprints, and evaluate technical, organizational, ethical, and global considerations.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in systems analysis, business analysis, product development, or IT project work where user needs must be translated into workable information-system designs.

title: The Art of Listening
courseDescription: Develops attentive and informed listening through guided study of Western music ranging from medieval chant to popular music. Students learn to recognize musical characteristics and connect what they hear with the cultural histories surrounding different works and styles.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want stronger critical-listening skills and a broader understanding of how music develops within historical and cultural contexts.

title: The Historian's Craft
courseDescription: Introduces the methods historians use to develop research questions, evaluate primary and secondary sources, and participate in historiographical debates. Students conduct independent historical research, assess evidence, and develop clear arguments through writing and other forms of communication.
whyRecommended: Recommended for history students who want practical experience conducting historical research and building evidence-based arguments from primary and scholarly sources.

title: Thermodynamics
courseDescription: Examines relationships among heat, work, and other forms of energy in engineering systems. Students analyze thermodynamic properties, phase changes, equations of state, the first and second laws of thermodynamics, entropy, and power and refrigeration cycles.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in mechanical, energy, thermal, or environmental engineering who need to analyze how energy is transferred and converted within engineered systems.

title: Travel Reporting
courseDescription: Explores contemporary forms of travel journalism while students develop their own stories based on places and experiences they encounter. Students practice narrative reporting, feature writing, critique, and revision while learning how journalists communicate the character of places and cultures to an audience.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in journalism, magazines, travel media, or feature writing who want experience turning firsthand observations into polished reported stories.
prerequisites: Restricted to students studying abroad during fall/spring

title: Upper-Level Language Course
courseDescription: Represents advanced 200- or 300-level language study rather than one specific Loyola course. Depending on the language and course, students strengthen advanced reading, writing, speaking, listening, and cultural or literary analysis while working increasingly in the target language.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to move beyond intermediate language proficiency and develop the advanced communication and cultural knowledge required for language majors and internationally focused work.
prerequisites: Varies by language and course; placement or completion of the appropriate preceding language course is required

title: Western Art: Renaissance to Contemporary
courseDescription: Surveys major Western artworks, artists, and artistic styles from the Renaissance through the present. Students learn to recognize important visual characteristics, compare artistic movements, and understand how works reflect the historical and cultural settings in which they were created.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in visual culture, museums, photography, studio art, or art history who want a broad foundation in Western artistic movements and visual analysis.

title: Special Topics in Professional Writing: Writing about Health
courseDescription: Examines health communication through the principles of professional and rhetorical writing. Students analyze how audience, purpose, context, and genre shape health information and practice adapting health-related material for different readers and communication situations.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students interested in medical writing, public health communication, or other health-related careers that require translating complex information into clear and audience-appropriate language.
prerequisites: WR 220 or written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Writing about Science
courseDescription: Teaches students to write science-based nonfiction for general audiences and analyze how popular discourse represents scientific ideas. Students read contemporary science writing, examine writers' rhetorical choices, and practice turning scientific material into clear, engaging public-facing prose without needing a prior science background.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to explain scientific material clearly to nontechnical readers in science, health, environmental, or public communication work.

title: Wet Ink: Writing and Editing for Publication
courseDescription: Surveys how publishing developed from the Gutenberg press to electronic books while giving students hands-on practice with editing and production from a writer's perspective. Students solicit original work, make editorial decisions, edit the selected writing, and produce a finished chapbook.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want a portfolio-ready publishing project and direct practice taking submitted writing from selection through editing and final production.

title: Digital Marketing and Analytics
courseDescription: Connects digital marketing technology to strategy, data, analytics, and customer insights across social media, CRM, direct marketing, content distribution, communications, and brand management. Students are introduced to platforms for direct marketing, CRM, web and social analytics, and data visualization, including Marketo, Salesforce, Adobe Omniture, Iconosquare, Tableau, or Power BI.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to turn data from digital channels into practical campaign, CRM, content, and brand decisions using marketing technology and analytics.

title: Content Marketing
courseDescription: Shows how organizations attract and retain customers through online content such as blogs and video, direct buyer communication, social sharing, and search-engine optimization. Students develop strategies for creating, distributing, measuring, and improving content so the intended audience can find and use it.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to plan discoverable online content, distribute it across channels, and use performance results to improve what a brand publishes.

title: Sports Marketing
courseDescription: Distinguishes marketing sports themselves from marketing other products and organizations through sports. Students compare amateur and professional and domestic and international contexts, then connect the development of sports marketing to current industry practices.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to understand how teams, leagues, events, athletes, and outside brands build and reach audiences through sports.

title: Customer Research and Analytics
courseDescription: Covers how marketers define research problems and collect primary and secondary data through focus groups, surveys, questionnaires, experiments, and qualitative or quantitative methods. Students organize and analyze data in Excel, interpret findings, and apply them to a real marketing decision through a group research project.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to design customer research, analyze real data, and turn findings into evidence-based product, audience, and marketing decisions.
prerequisites: EC 220, ST 110, ST 210, ST 265, or equivalent
Restricted to Business Administration majors with a Marketing concentration, Marketing majors, or Marketing minors

title: Strategic Marketing
courseDescription: Uses situational analysis, the marketing mix, segmentation, targeting, positioning, product-life-cycle analysis, and competitive conditions to evaluate and formulate marketing strategy. Students work in teams on case presentations and strategic marketing plans for firms operating amid global competition and uncertainty.
whyRecommended: Recommended for seniors who want to combine prior marketing knowledge into an execution-ready plan covering markets, positioning, product, price, place, and promotion.

title: New Product Development and Management
courseDescription: Walks students through the stages and strategy of developing and marketing new products, including product types, organizational structures for creativity, failure management, and technology-based innovation. Using design thinking, case studies, and hands-on teamwork, students conduct market research and develop an original innovation.
whyRecommended: Recommended for students who want to move a product idea through research, design, development, and go-to-market planning while learning how teams manage innovation and failure.

title: Stochastic Processes
courseDescription: Students model systems that change randomly using multivariate random variables, conditional probability, Poisson processes, Markov chains, birth-and-death processes, queues, random walks, and Brownian motion. They apply these models to analyze arrivals, waiting times, state transitions, congestion, and risks that evolve over time.
whyRecommended: The course develops probability-modeling skills used by quantitative analysts, risk analysts, operations researchers, and data scientists to analyze financial prices, customer queues, insurance events, and other uncertain systems.

title: Operations Research
courseDescription: Students translate routing, assignment, transportation, and resource-allocation problems into linear and combinatorial optimization models. They use the simplex algorithm, network flows, shortest-path methods, assignment models, and travelling-salesperson techniques to identify efficient solutions.
whyRecommended: These optimization methods are used by operations research analysts, supply-chain analysts, logistics analysts, and network planners to reduce costs, assign limited resources, and improve routes and capacity decisions.

title: Object-Oriented Data Structures
courseDescription: Students design programs with objects, classes, methods, inheritance, and polymorphism in a high-level object-oriented language. They implement linked lists, stacks, queues, maps, trees, searching, and sorting while evaluating whether their algorithms are correct and efficient.
whyRecommended: The programming, data-structure, and efficiency skills are used by software engineers, backend developers, and algorithm engineers when building fast applications, organizing application data, and solving technical interview problems.
prerequisites: Written permission of the department chair may substitute for students with an appropriate programming background

title: Computer Systems
courseDescription: Students write imperative programs in C within a GNU/Linux development environment and work directly with memory layout, memory management, and concurrency. They connect high-level code to assembly-language execution so they can identify performance, optimization, and security consequences.
whyRecommended: C, Linux, memory, and concurrency skills are used by systems programmers, cybersecurity engineers, embedded developers, and performance engineers to debug crashes, secure low-level code, and improve how programs use hardware.

title: Operating Systems
courseDescription: Students analyze how operating systems manage processes, concurrent execution, process synchronization, and mutual exclusion. They also work with memory allocation, CPU scheduling, disk management, current operating-system designs, and distributed operating systems.
whyRecommended: Process, memory, scheduling, and synchronization knowledge is used by systems engineers, cloud-infrastructure engineers, embedded developers, and operating-system developers when diagnosing deadlocks, resource bottlenecks, and performance failures.

title: Machine Learning
courseDescription: Students program supervised, unsupervised, and evolutionary learning methods and prepare data for use in machine-learning systems. They examine ethical issues and survey applications involving natural-language processing, computer vision, and robotics.
whyRecommended: Model-training and data-preparation skills are used by machine-learning engineers, data scientists, computer-vision engineers, and NLP engineers to build systems that classify data, detect patterns, and generate predictions.

title: Big Data
courseDescription: Students program systems for storing and processing datasets that are too large for conventional single-machine workflows. They learn how computing clusters are designed and administered and how large-scale machine-learning libraries process distributed data.
whyRecommended: Cluster and distributed-processing skills are used by data engineers, platform engineers, and big-data developers to operate analytics pipelines and machine-learning workloads that must run across multiple machines.
prerequisites: CS 212, CS 403, or DS 303; written permission of the instructor may substitute

title: Web Programming
courseDescription: Students develop browser interfaces with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and use server-side scripting languages to process user input. They connect client-side and server-side components while applying usability and functional-design principles to complete websites.
whyRecommended: These client-server skills are used by frontend, backend, and full-stack developers to build responsive interfaces, process forms, validate user input, and connect websites to server logic.

title: Mobile App Development
courseDescription: Students develop graphical interfaces and event-driven programs using Model-View-Controller architecture, structured data, and persistent storage. Their applications may incorporate games, graphics, sound, databases, or Android and iPhone development.
whyRecommended: MVC, event-driven interfaces, and persistent storage are used by iOS developers, Android developers, and software engineers when building interactive applications that save data and respond to user actions.

title: Graphical User Interface Design and Implementation
courseDescription: Students design, implement, and evaluate graphical interfaces for computer applications using human factors and established human-computer interaction standards. They practice event-driven programming and test whether interfaces let users complete tasks effectively and with fewer errors.
whyRecommended: Interface-design and usability-testing skills are used by UX engineers, interaction designers, usability analysts, and frontend developers to reduce user errors and make software easier to learn and operate.

title: Software Testing
courseDescription: Students evaluate whether software satisfies its stated requirements using static analysis, dynamic analysis, theoretical verification, and formal proofs. They classify errors, faults, and failures and work with test planning, quality assurance, consistency checks, and software-quality metrics.
whyRecommended: Testing and quality-assurance skills are used by QA engineers, software test engineers, quality analysts, and developers to catch defects before release and prove that software behaves according to its requirements.

title: Database Management Systems
courseDescription: Students design, implement, and use database-management systems while comparing logical organization, physical organization, and different database models. They define relational structures, retrieve and modify data with SQL, and use embedded SQL to connect database operations to application code.
whyRecommended: Relational design and SQL skills are used by database engineers, backend developers, data engineers, and data architects to build reliable storage systems, connect applications to data, and optimize how information is retrieved.

title: Computer Architecture
courseDescription: Students evaluate processor performance and design instruction sets, datapaths, arithmetic logic units, and control systems. They compare single-cycle, multicycle, and pipelined processors while working with hazard detection, forwarding, caches, virtual memory, peripherals, and input/output.
whyRecommended: Processor and memory-system design skills are used by computer architects, hardware engineers, embedded-systems engineers, and performance engineers to build processors, diagnose pipeline failures, and remove memory bottlenecks.
prerequisites: CS 371; or EG 071, EG 360, and EG 471

title: Introduction to Computer Networks
courseDescription: Students examine local-area networks, telecommunications, and how data moves through the physical, data-link, network, transport, and application layers. They analyze routing, IP internetworking, TCP transport, DNS, electronic mail, and the protocols supporting the Web.
whyRecommended: TCP/IP, routing, and protocol-analysis skills are used by network engineers, cloud-infrastructure engineers, security analysts, and backend developers to diagnose failed connections, routing problems, DNS errors, and network-performance issues.

title: Computer Graphics
courseDescription: Students use mathematics and graphics algorithms to generate two-dimensional and three-dimensional computer images. They program the modeling and display of objects, scenes, and lighting using high-level computer languages.
whyRecommended: Rendering, geometry, and scene-modeling skills are used by graphics programmers, game developers, visualization engineers, and simulation developers to display virtual objects, lighting, technical models, and interactive environments.
prerequisites: MA 301 or written permission of the instructor

title: Theory of Computation
courseDescription: Students construct finite-state machines, pushdown automata, and grammars to model how computational systems recognize and process inputs. They determine whether problems are computable, noncomputable, or NP-complete and evaluate the limits of possible algorithms.
whyRecommended: Formal-language and computability skills are used by compiler engineers, algorithm engineers, security researchers, and software engineers to design parsers, validate state-based systems, and identify problems that cannot be solved efficiently.

title: Cyber Security
courseDescription: Students identify common computer-security threats and analyze how they target devices, stored data, and networks. They implement basic protection systems and determine which safeguards address specific threat types.
whyRecommended: Threat-analysis and protection skills are used by security analysts, security engineers, incident responders, and systems administrators to harden devices, protect organizational data, and reduce network exposure.

title: Topics in Computer Science: Distributed Systems
courseDescription: Loyola offered Distributed Systems as a rotating CS 489 special topic in Spring 2024. Loyola's published record does not identify the programming language, platforms, assignments, or specific distributed-system techniques used in that offering, so those details cannot be added reliably.
whyRecommended: Distributed-systems study can support cloud, platform, backend, and site-reliability careers, but this entry should not recommend unverified tools or techniques until Loyola publishes another offering with detailed course content.
prerequisites: Junior or senior Computer Science major standing or written permission of the instructor

title: Introduction to Microprocessor-Based Systems
courseDescription: Students study how a modern microprocessor executes instructions through memory addressing, registers, stack pointers, arithmetic logic units, interrupts, and RISC architecture. They write assembly and C programs, interface software with physical hardware, use simulation and debugging tools, and complete a project on a 32-bit microprocessor.
whyRecommended: Microprocessor, C, assembly, and hardware-interfacing skills are used by embedded-systems engineers, firmware engineers, robotics engineers, and computer-hardware engineers to program controllers, connect sensors and peripherals, and debug hardware-software interactions.
prerequisites: EG 071 and EG 360 may be taken concurrently

title: Calculus III
courseDescription: Students calculate with vectors, three-dimensional surfaces, vector functions, partial derivatives, gradients, directional derivatives, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. They evaluate multiple, line, and surface integrals and apply Green's, Stokes', and divergence theorems in different coordinate systems.
whyRecommended: Multivariable and vector-calculus skills are used by mechanical, electrical, materials, and computer engineers, physicists, and quantitative analysts to model fields, motion, optimization problems, fluid flow, and systems with several changing variables.

title: Discrete Methods
courseDescription: Students write mathematical proofs using logical statements, natural-number properties, induction, sets, functions, and relations. They solve counting and probability problems with permutations, combinations, and other combinatorial arguments.
whyRecommended: Proof, induction, and combinatorial reasoning are used by algorithm engineers, software developers, data scientists, and quantitative researchers to prove program correctness, count possible outcomes, and evaluate complex decision spaces.

title: Analysis I
courseDescription: Students rebuild foundational calculus results from precise definitions and formal proofs rather than relying only on computational rules. They prove results involving the real number system, sequences, series, limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration of one-variable functions.
whyRecommended: Proof and convergence skills are used by mathematicians, quantitative researchers, and algorithm researchers when validating assumptions behind optimization methods, probability models, and numerical algorithms instead of relying only on software output.

title: Analysis II
courseDescription: Students extend proof-based calculus into advanced integration theory, improper integrals, infinite series, functions of several variables, and metric spaces. They determine when functions, integrals, sequences, and other infinite processes converge and prove why the resulting methods are valid.
whyRecommended: Advanced convergence and integration skills are used by mathematicians, quantitative researchers, and mathematical modelers to verify whether approximations, infinite-series methods, and multivariable models produce valid results.

title: Complex Analysis
courseDescription: Students calculate with complex numbers and analyze complex, analytic, and harmonic functions. They evaluate contour integrals and use Cauchy's Integral Formula, Laurent series, residues, and conformal mappings to solve problems involving complex-valued functions.
whyRecommended: Complex-function and contour-integration methods are used by applied mathematicians, physicists, electrical engineers, and quantitative researchers to analyze waves, fields, transforms, oscillations, and systems represented in the complex plane.

title: Numerical Analysis
courseDescription: Students develop stable and efficient algorithms for solving mathematical problems that may not have practical closed-form solutions. They implement direct and iterative linear-algebra methods, root-finding algorithms, and interpolation techniques used in scientific and engineering computation.
whyRecommended: Numerical-algorithm skills are used by computational scientists, simulation engineers, quantitative developers, and scientific software engineers to approximate solutions accurately while controlling runtime and numerical error.
prerequisites: MA 301 and MA 302; written permission of the instructor may substitute

title: Computational Mathematics
courseDescription: Students develop numerical algorithms for differentiation and for solving initial-value, two-point boundary-value, and partial differential equation problems. They evaluate whether computational solutions are stable and efficient enough for practical science and engineering applications.
whyRecommended: Differential-equation and numerical-computing skills are used by computational scientists, simulation engineers, quantitative developers, and mechanical engineers to model motion, heat, fluids, financial systems, and other processes that evolve over space or time.

title: Geometry
courseDescription: Students prove geometric results using formal axioms and compare Euclidean geometry with non-Euclidean systems. They may use coordinate geometry, linear algebra, and computer geometry systems to represent and investigate geometric structures.
whyRecommended: Geometric proof and modeling skills are used by mathematics educators, computational-geometry engineers, CAD developers, and mathematicians to validate spatial relationships and represent shapes in technical and software systems.

title: Combinatorics
courseDescription: Students count and organize discrete structures using bijections, multisets, multinomial coefficients, partitions, sequences, and distributions. They apply generating functions, inclusion-exclusion, partially ordered sets, and proof techniques to solve problems with many possible arrangements.
whyRecommended: Advanced counting methods are used by algorithm engineers, cryptographers, operations researchers, and quantitative researchers to measure possible outcomes, analyze discrete algorithms, schedule resources, and calculate combinatorial probabilities.
prerequisites: MA 351 or written permission of the instructor

title: Ring Theory
courseDescription: Students analyze the algebraic structures of integers, rings, polynomial systems, and fields. They use homomorphisms, cosets, and quotient structures to determine how algebraic systems relate and how their internal operations behave.
whyRecommended: Ring, field, and polynomial methods are used by mathematicians, cryptography researchers, coding-theory researchers, and algorithm researchers when designing algebraic encryption, error-correcting codes, and symbolic-computation systems.

title: Group Theory
courseDescription: Students analyze groups through homomorphisms, cosets, and quotient structures to describe symmetry and structure mathematically. Depending on the offering, they may apply these tools to Sylow theory, combinatorics, coding theory, or Galois theory.
whyRecommended: Symmetry and algebraic-structure methods are used by mathematicians, cryptographers, coding-theory researchers, and mathematical physicists to classify transformations, construct codes, and analyze systems whose behavior is preserved under specific operations.

title: Economics International Study Tour
courseDescription: Combines classroom economic analysis with an international study tour and organizational site visits in the Caribbean or Central America. Students compare economic theories with how businesses, public institutions, and communities respond to actual international market conditions.
whyRecommended: International economists, global market analysts, development consultants, and policy analysts use these observation and comparison skills to evaluate how local institutions, regulations, and economic conditions affect organizations operating abroad.
prerequisites: One 300-level or 400-level economics course, which may be taken concurrently
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Junior Analyst Class
courseDescription: Students use professional financial databases, interpret financial statements, construct financial models, and value stocks using multiple techniques. They convert their research into analyst reports and presentations that support an investment recommendation.
whyRecommended: Equity research analysts, investment analysts, credit analysts, and valuation analysts use these skills to turn company financial information into defensible valuations, recommendations, and client-ready reports.

title: Student Managed Sellinger Applied Portfolio Fund
courseDescription: Students serve as portfolio and investment managers for the Sellinger Applied Portfolio Fund while following the investment goals of Loyola's endowment. They make decisions involving asset valuation, investment constraints, asset allocation, security selection, risk management, behavioral finance, and portfolio-performance evaluation.
whyRecommended: Portfolio analysts, asset-management analysts, investment analysts, and fund researchers use these skills to select investments, construct portfolios, control risk, and explain performance to investment committees or clients.
prerequisites: FI 440, which may be taken concurrently
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Cost Accounting
courseDescription: Students measure, record, and forecast organizational costs using cost-volume-profit analysis, budgeting, relevant-cost analysis, and manufacturing costing systems. They identify which costs matter for a decision and apply cost information to pricing, production, budgeting, and operational planning.
whyRecommended: Cost accountants, management accountants, FP&A analysts, and operations analysts use these methods to calculate product costs, build budgets, evaluate margins, and determine whether operational decisions are financially worthwhile.

title: Taxation of Business Entities
courseDescription: Students calculate and compare the federal tax treatment of corporations, partnerships, and other flow-through entities. They examine taxable income, business deductions, depreciation, asset dispositions, entity distributions, income-tax accounting, multijurisdictional taxation, reorganizations, and how tax consequences affect the choice of business structure.
whyRecommended: Tax accountants, corporate tax analysts, forensic accountants, and tax consultants use these skills to calculate entity tax obligations, compare organizational structures, research tax issues, and identify the tax consequences of business transactions.

title: Auditing of Accounting Information Systems
courseDescription: Students examine how accounting information and assets move through transaction cycles and information systems. They document systems, identify internal-control weaknesses, evaluate technology-related risks, and assess whether an accounting process operates accurately and efficiently.
whyRecommended: IT auditors, internal auditors, accountants, and risk consultants use these skills to evaluate financial systems, identify control failures, protect transaction data, and recommend improvements to accounting processes.

title: Managing Talent
courseDescription: Students address workforce problems involving labor-market conditions, recruitment, selection, talent analytics, employment law, performance appraisal, training, labor relations, and employee retention. Cases, exercises, and team projects require students to make talent decisions from both manager and employee perspectives.
whyRecommended: Human-resources managers, talent-acquisition specialists, HR business partners, and people-analytics analysts use these skills to select employees, evaluate performance, plan development, and reduce costly turnover.

title: Managing Teams
courseDescription: Students practice collaborative behaviors, establish conditions for effective teamwork, and address problems that prevent teams from performing reliably. Exercises, simulations, case studies, and team projects require them to facilitate decisions and develop flexible responses to changing problems.
whyRecommended: Project managers, management consultants, operations managers, and team leaders use these skills to assign responsibilities, improve collaboration, resolve team-performance problems, and keep group projects moving toward measurable outcomes.

title: Management Consulting Practicum
courseDescription: Students diagnose complex organizational problems, formulate strategic solutions, and develop recommendations for organizations. They apply the consulting process to cases involving corporate strategy, leadership, organizational effectiveness, international business, and sustainable development.
whyRecommended: Management consultants, strategy analysts, corporate-development analysts, and organizational-effectiveness consultants use these skills to structure ambiguous client problems, evaluate evidence, develop implementable recommendations, and defend those recommendations to decision-makers.

title: Management
courseDescription: Students examine how personality, ability, motivation, job attitudes, stress, relationships, and learning affect employee performance and well-being. They apply organizational-behavior concepts to leadership, teamwork, power, workplace culture, and management decisions through cases, assessments, simulations, and team projects.
whyRecommended: Managers, HR business partners, management consultants, and project leaders use these concepts to motivate employees, diagnose workplace problems, organize effective teams, and select leadership practices that fit an organization's culture.

title: Introduction to Communication Disorders
courseDescription: Surveys speech, language, and hearing disorders affecting children, adolescents, and adults. Students learn to distinguish major categories of communication impairment and connect observable communication difficulties with the assessment, clinical, and educational work performed by speech-language and hearing professionals.
whyRecommended: Speech-language pathologists, audiologists, speech-language pathology assistants, and clinical research coordinators use this foundation to recognize communication difficulties, understand referral needs, and communicate accurately about speech, language, and hearing conditions.

title: Hearing Science and Acoustics
courseDescription: Introduces acoustics and psychoacoustics as they apply to hearing and communication. Students examine the peripheral and central auditory systems and connect pathological changes in those systems to problems with hearing and sound perception.
whyRecommended: Audiologists, hearing scientists, speech-language pathologists, and hearing instrument specialists use acoustic and psychoacoustic analysis to explain how sound reaches the auditory system and how hearing disorders affect communication.

title: Phonetics
courseDescription: Examines how speech sounds are produced and teaches students to transcribe speech using the International Phonetic Alphabet. Students practice distinguishing speech sounds by ear and analyzing rule-based differences associated with dialects, idiolects, and speech disorders.
whyRecommended: Speech-language pathologists, pathology assistants, linguists, and accent or dialect coaches use phonetic transcription and auditory discrimination to document pronunciation accurately and identify meaningful speech-sound patterns.

title: Observation Methods and Techniques in Speech-Language Pathology/Audiology
courseDescription: Provides direct observation of clinical work involving clients of different ages with speech, language, swallowing, and hearing problems. Students observe at Loyola Clinical Centers and, when feasible, off-campus sites while repeatedly editing observation reports to develop accurate preclinical documentation.
whyRecommended: Speech-language pathologists, audiologists, pathology assistants, and clinical research coordinators use these observation and report-writing skills to document client behavior, treatment procedures, and clinical outcomes without confusing observation with interpretation.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Speech and Language Development
courseDescription: Covers typical speech and language development from birth through adolescence. Students examine phonological, morphological, semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic development, including acquisition sequences and the effects of social and cultural environments on communication.
whyRecommended: Pediatric speech-language pathologists, early-intervention specialists, child-development specialists, and special-education teachers use developmental sequences to compare a child's communication with expected milestones and determine when further evaluation or support is appropriate.

title: Anatomy and Physiology: Speech and Voice
courseDescription: Examines the structures and functions responsible for normal speech production, with detailed study of respiration, phonation, and articulation. Students also receive introductory instruction in communication-related neuroanatomy and swallowing.
whyRecommended: Medical speech-language pathologists, voice therapists, speech scientists, and singing-voice specialists use this anatomy to determine how respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory systems contribute to speech and voice symptoms.

title: Articulation and Phonological Disorders
courseDescription: Applies current theories and evidence-based methods to the assessment and treatment of speech-sound disorders. Students identify articulation errors and phonological processes while distinguishing disorders from differences related to dialect, bilingualism, and childhood organic or neurogenic conditions.
whyRecommended: Pediatric and school-based speech-language pathologists, pathology assistants, and communication-disorders researchers use these skills to classify speech-sound errors, select appropriate treatment targets, and avoid misidentifying dialectal or bilingual differences as disorders.

title: Clinical Audiology
courseDescription: Examines behavioral and electrophysiological assessment of the auditory and balance systems, including middle-ear analysis, speech audiometry, and site-of-lesion testing. Students interpret assessment data in laboratory exercises and write clinical reports that support differential diagnosis and appropriate referrals.
whyRecommended: Audiologists, audiology assistants, hearing instrument specialists, and clinical research coordinators use these assessment and documentation skills to interpret hearing-test results, differentiate possible disorder locations, and communicate diagnostic findings.

title: Speech Science
courseDescription: Provides advanced study of the physiology and acoustics of speech and voice production together with current speech-perception research. In collaborative laboratory sessions, students use speech-measurement technology to analyze acoustic properties of normal and disordered speech.
whyRecommended: Speech scientists, speech-language pathologists, voice researchers, and acoustics researchers use these laboratory and measurement skills to compare speech signals, examine voice production, and interpret measurable differences between normal and disordered speech.

title: Neurology for Communication Sciences and Disorders
courseDescription: Traces normal neurological and physiological development from neuroembryology through adulthood. Students examine the nervous-system structures and processes that support speech, language, and cognition.
whyRecommended: Medical speech-language pathologists, neurorehabilitation clinicians, communication-neuroscience researchers, and speech-language pathology researchers use functional neuroanatomy to connect speech, language, and cognitive symptoms with affected neurological systems.

title: Aural Habilitation
courseDescription: Examines how hearing impairment affects communication for children and adults, including relevant social and emotional consequences. Students evaluate assessment, intervention, habilitation, rehabilitation, and educational options for people with hearing loss.
whyRecommended: Audiologists, speech-language pathologists, aural-rehabilitation specialists, and teachers of deaf and hard-of-hearing students use these skills to assess communication needs and select workable intervention or educational approaches for people with hearing loss.
relatedCareers: Teacher of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomore, junior, or senior Speech-Language-Hearing Sciences majors

title: Child and Adolescent Communication Disorders
courseDescription: Examines childhood and adolescent communication disorders using strength-based and neurodiversity-informed approaches. Students analyze case studies, connect physical, neurological, and social-emotional factors to communication needs, and develop practical treatment solutions.
whyRecommended: Pediatric and school-based speech-language pathologists, pathology assistants, and child-language researchers use these case-analysis skills to identify client strengths, explain communication difficulties, and plan appropriate interventions.

title: Neurological Bases of Adult Communication Disorders
courseDescription: Examines acquired adult neurological disorders including aphasia, right-hemisphere disorder, traumatic brain injury, dementia, and motor-speech disorders. Students use case-based activities and a cognitive-screening tool to connect neuroanatomy with communication symptoms and clinical decisions.
whyRecommended: Medical speech-language pathologists, neurorehabilitation clinicians, cognitive-communication specialists, and clinical researchers use these skills to screen adult cognition, interpret neurogenic symptoms, and plan further assessment or treatment.

title: Biomechanics of Sports and Exercise
courseDescription: Applies classical mechanics to human movement and other biological problems. Students examine how the musculoskeletal system functions internally and calculate how external forces affect the body's motion during sports and exercise.
whyRecommended: Biomechanical engineers, sports scientists, rehabilitation engineers, and human-movement researchers use these skills to analyze athletic motion, musculoskeletal loading, movement efficiency, and injury mechanisms.
prerequisites: None in the last catalogued version; current prerequisite status could not be verified

title: Physics of Medicine and the Human Body
courseDescription: Applies mechanics, fluid physics, and sound to biomechanics, metabolism, circulation, respiration, and hearing. Students also examine the physical operation of MRI, PET, gamma-camera, and related medical instruments through hands-on activities.
whyRecommended: Medical physicists, biomedical engineers, imaging specialists, and clinical engineering technologists use these principles to explain body-system measurements and evaluate how diagnostic instruments produce medically useful information.

title: Waves and the Physics of Medicine
courseDescription: Applies geometric optics, light-tissue interactions, nuclear physics, and ultrasound to medical technology. Students examine how fiber optics, CT, gamma cameras, PET, MRI, and ultrasound systems form images or collect diagnostic information.
whyRecommended: Medical physicists, imaging scientists, biomedical engineers, and ultrasound-system engineers use these wave and imaging principles to understand instrument operation, image formation, and interactions between energy and human tissue.

title: Modern Physics
courseDescription: Introduces special relativity and quantum physics through calculable physical models. Students work with Lorentz transformations, mass-energy equivalence, wave-particle duality, uncertainty, quantized energy and angular momentum, atomic orbitals, and the infinite-square-well model.
whyRecommended: Physicists, quantum-technology researchers, aerospace engineers, and semiconductor engineers use these models to analyze high-speed systems and matter at atomic or quantum scales.

title: Classical Mechanics
courseDescription: Develops Newtonian models for particles, multi-particle systems, and rigid bodies moving in two and three dimensions. Students translate physical systems into equations that predict forces, acceleration, rotation, momentum, and mechanical motion.
whyRecommended: Mechanical and aerospace engineers, roboticists, simulation engineers, and physicists use these models to predict vehicle motion, machinery behavior, robotic movement, and interacting mechanical systems.

title: Thermal Physics
courseDescription: Examines temperature, heat, entropy, free energy, and thermodynamic cycles used to describe energy transfer and system efficiency. Students also apply probability, statistical physics, and kinetic gas theory to the behavior of large collections of particles.
whyRecommended: Thermal engineers, energy-systems engineers, mechanical engineers, and materials scientists use these calculations to evaluate engines, refrigeration systems, energy conversion, material behavior, and heat-driven processes.

title: Quantum Mechanics I
courseDescription: Develops quantum-mechanical models based on the Schrödinger wave equation and its solutions for physically important systems. Students apply the equation to atomic and molecular physics and interpret how wave functions describe measurable quantum behavior.
whyRecommended: Quantum physicists, atomic physicists, materials scientists, and quantum-technology researchers use Schrödinger-equation models to predict energy states and analyze atomic, molecular, and nanoscale systems.
prerequisites: PH 307 and PH 312, or written permission of the department chair

title: Electricity and Magnetism I
courseDescription: Uses Maxwell's equations to describe electricity and magnetism in free space. Students calculate electric and magnetic fields produced by charge and current distributions and model the creation and propagation of electromagnetic waves.
whyRecommended: Electromagnetics engineers, RF engineers, photonics engineers, and physicists use these calculations to design antennas, analyze wireless signals, model optical systems, and predict electromagnetic-field behavior.
prerequisites: PH 316 or written permission of the department chair

title: Physics Research
courseDescription: Provides a faculty-supervised physics research project ending with a public presentation of the results. Students carry out an investigation, analyze evidence, document their conclusions, and communicate the completed work to an audience.
whyRecommended: Research physicists, laboratory assistants, research engineers, and graduate researchers use these skills to complete independent investigations, evaluate experimental or theoretical results, and present defensible scientific conclusions.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Introduction to Engineering Materials
courseDescription: Examines how bonding, crystal structure, defects, phase transformations, and electrical behavior determine material properties. Students compare metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites and use mechanical behavior and phase diagrams to evaluate materials for engineering applications.
whyRecommended: Materials, mechanical, manufacturing, and quality engineers use structure-property relationships and phase diagrams to select materials, anticipate failures, and match components with operating conditions.

title: Materials Science Lab
courseDescription: Uses hands-on experiments and data analysis to reinforce concepts from EG 351. Students investigate crystallography, mechanical properties, phase diagrams, viscosity, solidification structures, and the effects of temperature on material deformation and fracture.
whyRecommended: Materials-testing engineers, laboratory engineers, quality engineers, and failure-analysis engineers use these techniques to measure material behavior, interpret test results, and document evidence supporting material decisions.

title: Solid Mechanics Laboratory
courseDescription: Combines laboratory testing with mechanics-of-materials analysis. Students measure stress and strain, examine elastic and plastic deformation, test mechanical properties, investigate buckling and stress concentrations, and apply results to simple mechanical designs.
whyRecommended: Mechanical test engineers, structural analysts, materials engineers, and product-design engineers use these methods to measure component behavior, validate mechanical calculations, and identify conditions that can cause deformation or failure.

title: Introduction to Digital Circuits and Systems Laboratory
courseDescription: Provides laboratory practice supporting EG 471 using multimeters, power supplies, function generators, and digital oscilloscopes. Students build and test logic gates, combinational circuits, N-bit adders, flip-flops, and sequential logic while following electrical-laboratory safety procedures.
whyRecommended: Hardware test engineers, electronics laboratory engineers, FPGA engineers, and embedded-hardware engineers use these skills to assemble digital circuits, operate measurement equipment, locate faults, and verify that hardware behaves as designed.
prerequisites: EG 140 or CS 151 may be taken concurrently

title: Engineering Design Project I
courseDescription: Begins the senior engineering capstone with multidisciplinary team planning for an open-ended design problem connected to a societal need. Students define requirements, compare design alternatives, establish performance specifications, and produce a project plan, schedule, oral presentation, and technical documentation.
whyRecommended: Design engineers, systems engineers, project engineers, and engineering project managers use these skills to convert broad problems into specifications, compare feasible solutions, and organize technical work before fabrication begins.
prerequisites: At least one EG 400-level concentration elective

title: Engineering Design Project II
courseDescription: Completes the senior capstone by requiring teams to finalize, fabricate, and test the designs planned in EG 497. Students build a working product, conduct verification tests, analyze data, control project spending, document lessons learned, and present the final results.
whyRecommended: Product-development engineers, test engineers, systems engineers, and engineering project managers use these skills to turn specifications into working prototypes, verify performance, manage costs, and communicate completed project results.

title: 3-D Design in Art and Engineering
courseDescription: Combines studio-art methods with engineering approaches to three-dimensional and spatial design. Students create physical work using multiple fabrication methods while learning visual communication, engineering drawing, computer-aided solid modeling, and 3-D printing.
whyRecommended: Product designers, industrial designers, 3-D artists, and CAD designers use these skills to turn spatial concepts into digital models, fabricated prototypes, and clearly communicated visual designs.
prerequisites: Closed to students who have taken EG 426

title: Introduction to Creative Nonfiction
courseDescription: Introduces conventional and experimental approaches to writing fact-based stories. Students read and analyze nonfiction and produce revised work in forms such as personal essays, profiles, and short nonfiction, building a portfolio through feedback and continued editing.
whyRecommended: Essayists, journalists, content writers, and communications specialists use these techniques to turn factual experiences and interviews into accurate, engaging stories for publications, organizations, and digital audiences.

title: Introduction to Rhetoric
courseDescription: Examines how historical and contemporary writers use rhetorical strategies to persuade different audiences. Students analyze and produce nonfiction that accounts for the writer's purpose, intended audience, chosen form, and surrounding social context.
whyRecommended: Public-relations specialists, policy writers, communications strategists, and advocacy specialists use rhetorical analysis to identify audience expectations, construct persuasive arguments, and adapt messages to professional and civic settings.

title: Argumentation
courseDescription: Examines how arguments operate in personal conversations, academic writing, journalism, advertising, and political controversies. Students break arguments into claims, evidence, assumptions, and counterarguments, evaluate published examples, and build persuasive arguments that can withstand informed opposition.
whyRecommended: Attorneys and policy analysts use these skills to identify weak reasoning and defend recommendations with evidence. Editorial writers and communications strategists apply the same methods when preparing persuasive articles, campaign messages, policy briefs, and responses to opposing claims.

title: Gendered Rhetoric
courseDescription: Studies how gender has shaped which speaking and writing styles receive authority in public life. Students analyze speeches, essays, media messages, and public debates to identify gendered assumptions, examine who is permitted to speak with authority, and design messages that communicate effectively without repeating exclusionary conventions.
whyRecommended: Advocacy writers and public affairs specialists use gender-aware rhetorical analysis to prevent campaigns from alienating audiences or reproducing stereotypes. Speechwriters and communications researchers apply these skills when evaluating whose voices are represented, adapting language for different communities, and developing inclusive public messages.

title: Speech Writing and Delivery
courseDescription: Applies classical rhetoric and Loyola's tradition of eloquentia perfecta to professional speaking. Students research topics, write informative and persuasive speeches, adapt language and evidence to specific audiences, rehearse delivery, speak individually and in teams, and revise presentations using audience and peer feedback.
whyRecommended: Executive communications specialists and speechwriters use these skills to produce remarks that sound natural when spoken and support a leader's objectives. Public affairs professionals and political communications strategists use audience analysis, delivery practice, and persuasive organization for press conferences, campaign events, hearings, and community presentations.

title: The Contemporary Essay
courseDescription: Explores the essay as a working form for contemporary thought rather than only as an academic assignment. Students closely read published essayists, examine how writers combine observation, research, reflection, voice, and structure, and produce revised essays suitable for magazines, literary publications, or a professional portfolio.
whyRecommended: Magazine writers and essayists use these techniques to turn research and personal observation into publishable nonfiction. Editors and cultural critics apply close reading, structural analysis, and revision skills when developing features, reviewing submissions, and explaining social or cultural subjects to general audiences.

title: Multimedia Storytelling
courseDescription: Provides practical training in building stories for news, persuasion, and entertainment with coordinated text, images, audio, video, and digital presentation. Students select media based on what each part contributes to the story, organize material for a defined audience, produce multimedia packages, and evaluate how production choices affect audience understanding.
whyRecommended: Multimedia journalists use these skills to combine interviews, written reporting, photographs, and video into complete digital stories. Digital content producers, communications specialists, and social media producers apply the same workflow when creating campaign features, organization profiles, event coverage, and cross-platform content packages.

title: Radio Storytelling
courseDescription: Teaches broadcast production and writing for stories designed to be heard rather than read. Students research and script audio stories, conduct recorded interviews, collect natural sound, organize narration and clips, edit complete segments, and prepare material for radio, podcast, and digital-audio distribution.
whyRecommended: Radio reporters and audio journalists use these skills to turn field interviews and recorded sound into accurate deadline-driven stories. Podcast producers and broadcast producers apply audio scripting, recording, and editing when creating news segments, documentary episodes, interview programs, and branded audio.

title: Advanced TV Reporting and News Producing
courseDescription: Operates as an applied television newsroom in which students develop stories about Loyola and Baltimore, report and script video packages, coordinate interviews and footage, and assemble stories into a produced newscast. Students practice the reporting, editorial judgment, production coordination, and deadline management required to move a television story from pitch to broadcast.
whyRecommended: Television reporters and multimedia journalists use these skills to research, write, record, and edit complete news packages. News producers and assignment editors apply the course's newsroom coordination and editorial judgment when selecting stories, organizing a program, managing deadlines, and preparing material for broadcast.

title: Documentary Production
courseDescription: Guides students through the production of documentaries focused on domestic diversity and community subjects. Students research a subject, develop a documentary approach, write production material, conduct interviews, record video and sound, edit a coherent nonfiction narrative, and present the completed documentary to an audience.
whyRecommended: Documentary filmmakers and field producers use these skills to research subjects, secure meaningful interviews, and organize unscripted footage into a factual story. Video producers and documentary editors apply the same production process to nonprofit films, public-history projects, news documentaries, community profiles, and streaming content.

title: Arts and Entertainment Media
courseDescription: Examines and produces media coverage of arts and culture, including style, food, film, music, technology, and emerging cultural trends. Students evaluate professional coverage, research artists and cultural subjects, conduct interviews, and develop reviews and reported features for print or digital publication.
whyRecommended: Arts journalists and entertainment reporters use these skills to research cultural subjects, interview creators, and write informed reviews and features under publication deadlines. Culture editors and media critics apply them when evaluating pitches, checking cultural context, editing coverage, and distinguishing supported criticism from unsupported opinion.

title: Introduction to Communication
courseDescription: Introduces the history, theories, practices, institutions, and social effects of modern communication media in the United States. Students examine how audiences experience media, how media organizations produce and distribute content, how communication influences society, and how professional roles operate across journalism, advertising, public relations, and digital media.
whyRecommended: Communications specialists and public relations professionals use this foundation to understand how messages move through media organizations and reach different audiences. Journalists and media analysts apply it when assessing ownership, industry incentives, audience behavior, and the social consequences of news and entertainment content.

title: Fundamentals of Advertising and Public Relations
courseDescription: Provides a working foundation in advertising and public relations as connected parts of strategic communication. Students identify audiences, apply persuasion and social-influence research, develop communication objectives and message strategies, and evaluate ethical, regulatory, and social-responsibility issues across traditional and emerging media.
whyRecommended: Advertising account executives use these skills to translate client goals into audience, message, and channel decisions. Public relations specialists, campaign coordinators, and communications strategists apply them when preparing briefs, planning integrated campaigns, checking legal and ethical risks, and explaining recommendations to clients or organizational leaders.

title: Writing for Public Relations
courseDescription: Trains students to produce the materials public relations professionals deliver to journalists, employees, clients, and other stakeholders. Assignments include press releases, speeches, organizational background material, position papers, newsletters, and other audience-specific communications that must be accurate, concise, and ready for professional use.
whyRecommended: Public relations and media-relations specialists use these skills to prepare releases, pitches, backgrounders, and spokesperson material that journalists can use quickly. Corporate communications specialists and public information officers apply them when explaining organizational decisions, preparing executive remarks, and distributing consistent information during routine announcements or public scrutiny.

title: Case Studies in Public Relations
courseDescription: Uses real cases from corporations, government agencies, educational institutions, and nonprofit organizations to examine public relations management. Students reconstruct why practitioners selected particular strategies, evaluate campaign results, identify psychological, ethical, and legal problems, and recommend better responses for comparable communication situations.
whyRecommended: Public relations account managers use case analysis to recognize campaign risks before recommending strategy to a client. Crisis communications specialists, corporate communications managers, and public affairs specialists apply the course's decision framework when comparing response options, anticipating stakeholder reactions, and defending a communication plan to organizational leadership.

title: Social Media Strategies
courseDescription: Applies social media to advertising and public relations objectives such as promoting products, managing organizational identity, and building community relationships. Students study professional practices in audience tracking, campaign measurement, search engine optimization, content planning, and platform selection, then develop a complete social media campaign.
whyRecommended: Social media strategists and digital communications specialists use these skills to turn organizational goals into content calendars, audience targets, channel choices, and measurable campaign objectives. Community managers and content strategists apply performance data and search practices to improve discoverability, engagement, response planning, and future content decisions.

title: Advertising Culture and Identity
courseDescription: Examines how consumers' personal and social identities influence their responses to advertising and how commercial messages can shape or reflect identity. Students evaluate the relationship between audience characteristics, campaign messages, advertising outcomes, and cultural representation.
whyRecommended: Advertising strategists, brand planners, and consumer insights analysts use these skills to evaluate audience reactions, identify stereotyping, and adapt campaigns for specific cultural and demographic groups.

title: Media Relations
courseDescription: Develops the techniques needed to manage an organization's relationships with journalists and other media professionals. Students build communication plans and practice acting as organizational spokespersons through scenario-based media exercises.
whyRecommended: Media relations specialists, public information officers, press secretaries, and PR account executives use these skills to prepare spokespersons, respond to reporters, and communicate an organization's position during interviews or breaking events.

title: Health Communication
courseDescription: Applies communication theory to health outcomes through case studies, collaborative work, and service-learning. Students evaluate health communication across patient, cultural, organizational, public, political, risk, crisis, advertising, and public-relations settings while considering systemic, ethical, and social-justice factors.
whyRecommended: Health communication specialists, hospital communications teams, public health campaign coordinators, and healthcare PR professionals use these skills to adapt health information for different audiences and communicate effectively during outreach or health crises.
prerequisites: CM 307 or written permission of the instructor

title: Mobile Media and UX Design
courseDescription: Examines how smartphone applications and other mobile media affect daily life, economies, and global society. Students apply mobile user-experience and design principles by prototyping app concepts, creating mobile-optimized content, and evaluating current mobile web and application design trends.
whyRecommended: UX designers, mobile product designers, interaction designers, and content designers use these skills to prototype app experiences, organize content for small screens, and make mobile products easier to navigate.

title: Video I
courseDescription: Introduces digital video production through practical work with cameras, lighting, editing, basic animation, and studio equipment. Students learn to produce video for broadcast, streaming, and other digital-media formats.
whyRecommended: Videographers, video editors, multimedia producers, and production assistants use these skills to operate cameras, light scenes, assemble footage, and prepare video content for digital or broadcast distribution.

title: Video II
courseDescription: Advances video storytelling through complete productions developed from original movie concepts. Students write full scripts, recruit and rehearse actors, direct shoots, edit footage, and prepare finished videos for public presentation.
whyRecommended: Filmmakers, directors, video producers, and editors use this script-to-screen experience to manage performers, coordinate production decisions, and deliver finished narrative videos.

title: Graphics II
courseDescription: Develops publication design, layout, and production skills using industry-standard computer tools. Students create and refine formats, grids, page layouts, logos, nameplates, and typography so that visual design communicates information clearly.
whyRecommended: Graphic designers, publication designers, art directors, and production designers use these skills to construct readable page systems, control visual hierarchy, and prepare consistent publications for clients or editorial teams.

title: Comics Creation
courseDescription: Students create comics as visual narratives and prepare completed work for presentation in class projects such as a comics anthology. Course materials and assignments incorporate culturally diverse artists and perspectives while students develop their own combinations of sequential images and written language.
whyRecommended: Comic artists, graphic novelists, storyboard artists, and illustrators use these skills to organize narratives across sequential images, coordinate words with artwork, and prepare completed visual stories for readers or publishers.
prerequisites: Current prerequisite not published in Loyola's public course sources

title: Podcasting and Long-Form Digital Audio
courseDescription: Develops creative audio-storytelling techniques through the production of podcasts and long-form features. Students pitch and research stories, conduct interviews, record in the field, write scripts, and complete multitrack editing and production for radio and digital platforms.
whyRecommended: Podcast producers, audio journalists, narrative producers, and audio editors use these skills to find viable stories, capture strong interviews and field sound, and turn recorded material into polished long-form programs.

title: Book Design and Production
courseDescription: Applies long-form visual-communication principles to computer-aided book design and layout. Students collaborate with authors and editors to develop cover and interior designs for books published by Loyola's Apprentice House Press.
whyRecommended: Book designers, publication designers, production artists, and art directors use these skills to translate manuscripts into coordinated cover and interior systems while working with authors, editors, and publishing schedules.

title: Creative Media Producing
courseDescription: Develops creative storytelling and production skills for broadcast and digital media. Students create sports, news, talk, entertainment, feature, and reality programming while practicing both on-air and behind-the-scenes production responsibilities.
whyRecommended: Broadcast producers, television producers, sports media producers, and digital content producers use these skills to develop program concepts, coordinate production roles, and move media projects from planning to distribution.

title: Free Speech, Free Expression
courseDescription: Uses major U.S. Supreme Court decisions to examine the boundaries of free speech and expression. Students analyze the relationship between speech and democracy, possible restrictions on public debate, and First Amendment protections for commercial communication.
whyRecommended: Journalists, media attorneys, communications policy analysts, and public-relations leaders use these skills to distinguish protected expression from regulated speech and evaluate the legal risks surrounding public or commercial messages.

title: Social Media and Culture
courseDescription: Examines how social media and emerging technologies shape cultural meaning and personal and professional experiences. Students analyze connections among content creation, marketing, promotion, fan communities, influencers, audience engagement, and social change.
whyRecommended: Social media strategists, influencer marketing specialists, audience engagement managers, and cultural researchers use these skills to interpret online communities, select credible creators, and anticipate how digital campaigns affect public behavior.

title: Stereotypes in U.S. Media
courseDescription: Uses critical-cultural methods to examine how films, documentaries, television, online media, and music videos construct racial, gender, and class images. Students analyze how these representations shape perceptions, biases, and behavior and consider how media creators can produce more respectful visual representations.
whyRecommended: Inclusive marketing strategists, documentary producers, media researchers, and cultural critics use these skills to identify harmful representations, audit creative work for bias, and develop imagery that communicates across diverse audiences.

title: Exploring Digital Culture
courseDescription: Examines how internet platforms influence identity, relationships, thinking, marketing, politics, and culture. Students evaluate the social, economic, intellectual, and legal effects of digital services through issues such as privacy, civility, free speech, online identity, and public policy.
whyRecommended: Digital policy analysts, media researchers, digital strategists, and trust and safety analysts use these skills to evaluate platform behavior, identify privacy and identity risks, and explain how internet technologies affect organizations and communities.

title: Introduction to Public Policy
courseDescription: Examines how public policy is developed and implemented within the American political system. Students analyze how issues reach the national agenda, where policy alternatives originate, and how government officials, institutions, interest groups, and other actors influence decisions.
whyRecommended: Policy analysts, legislative analysts, government affairs specialists, and public-sector consultants use these skills to track proposals through the policy process, identify influential stakeholders, and explain why particular alternatives gain political support.

title: State and Local Politics and Policymaking
courseDescription: Examines how state governments make policy within the American federal system. Students compare political institutions and policymaking across states and analyze how authority and responsibility shift between state and federal governments.
whyRecommended: State policy analysts, legislative aides, municipal policy advisors, and state government affairs specialists use these skills to compare state laws, monitor intergovernmental conflicts, and adapt policy proposals to different state institutions.

title: Analytical and Legal Reasoning
courseDescription: Uses judicial politics, legal theory, and rhetoric to examine the relationship between law and reason. Students practice breaking arguments into claims, assumptions, evidence, and conclusions while developing reasoning skills applicable to legal study and the LSAT.
whyRecommended: Attorneys, judicial law clerks, legal analysts, and legislative policy advisors use these skills to test arguments, identify unsupported assumptions, interpret competing legal positions, and construct defensible conclusions.

title: Constitutional Law: Federalism and Separation of Powers
courseDescription: Examines the constitutional principles that organize and limit governmental power. Students analyze how federalism divides authority between national and state governments and how separation of powers distributes authority among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
whyRecommended: Constitutional attorneys, legislative counsel, government attorneys, and judicial law clerks use these skills to determine which institution has legal authority and whether government action exceeds constitutional limits.

title: Constitutional Law: Individual Liberties
courseDescription: Examines the constitutional principles governing relationships between individuals and government. Students focus on how the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment restrict government action and protect individual rights.
whyRecommended: Civil-rights attorneys, public defenders, constitutional attorneys, and policy analysts use these skills to evaluate government restrictions, identify unequal treatment, and assess whether laws satisfy due-process and equal-protection requirements.

title: Politics of the Judicial Process
courseDescription: Examines how judicial systems operate at the national, state, and local levels and how courts interact with other political institutions. Students analyze how institutional relationships and political pressures shape judicial authority, decisions, and public policy.
whyRecommended: Judicial law clerks, court administrators, legal analysts, and public policy analysts use this knowledge to follow cases through court systems, explain judicial authority, and assess how rulings affect policy.

title: Interest Groups and Lobbying
courseDescription: Examines how interest groups form, maintain support, lobby government, influence elections, and represent constituencies within a democracy. Students evaluate the practical strategies lobbyists and advocacy organizations use to influence legislators, elections, and public policy.
whyRecommended: Lobbyists, government relations specialists, advocacy directors, and political consultants use these skills to build coalitions, monitor legislation, plan lobbying campaigns, and influence electoral and policy decisions.

title: Contemporary Campaigns and Elections
courseDescription: Examines modern political campaigns, electoral strategy, and campaign finance. Students evaluate campaign plans, electoral conditions, and the financial structures that candidates and organizations must navigate when competing for office.
whyRecommended: Campaign managers, political consultants, campaign finance analysts, and field organizers use these skills to develop electoral strategies, allocate campaign resources, evaluate political conditions, and follow campaign-finance requirements.

title: Comparative Politics
courseDescription: Introduces the systematic comparison of countries and their domestic political, economic, and social systems. Students use cross-national evidence to compare institutions and explain why governance structures and policy outcomes differ between countries.
whyRecommended: Comparative political analysts, country risk analysts, international policy analysts, and foreign affairs researchers use cross-national comparison to assess political institutions, compare governance environments, and explain different policy outcomes.

title: International Politics
courseDescription: Examines major arguments about the causes of war and peace, the continuing risk of conflict between states, and the role of human rights in international affairs. Students also evaluate whether globalization and international trade encourage cooperation or create new sources of conflict.
whyRecommended: Foreign policy analysts, diplomats, geopolitical risk analysts, and international affairs specialists use these frameworks to assess conflicts, prepare policy briefings, evaluate international risks, and recommend diplomatic responses.

title: Global Politics of Migration
courseDescription: Introduces major approaches to international migration and examines immigration's effects on receiving countries. Students work with migration data and course evidence to evaluate claims about cross-border movement, host-country outcomes, and migration policy.
whyRecommended: Migration policy analysts, immigration policy specialists, refugee program officers, and international organization analysts use these skills to interpret migration data, evaluate regulations and programs, and assess humanitarian and host-country impacts.

title: Politics of the Middle East
courseDescription: Examines Middle Eastern politics from a comparative perspective, including the region's political systems and its importance to outside powers such as the United States and Russia. Students compare countries and regional power relationships to interpret alliances, political developments, and international policy decisions.
