whyRecommended: Middle East policy analysts, diplomats, intelligence analysts, and international affairs specialists use regional comparison and power analysis to prepare country briefings, interpret alliances, and assess political developments.

title: Law and Religion
courseDescription: Examines the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses of the First Amendment and the legal boundaries between government and religion. Students analyze constitutional disputes involving government support of religion, religious liberty, and laws that burden religious practices.
whyRecommended: Constitutional attorneys, religious liberty counsel, civil rights policy analysts, and legislative analysts use this knowledge to review proposed policies, construct constitutional arguments, and assess church-state legal risks.

title: Arabic IV
courseDescription: Continues Arabic III by strengthening fourth-semester speaking, listening, reading, and writing proficiency. Students complete structured language work inside and outside the classroom, while heritage speakers consult the instructor to determine appropriate placement.
whyRecommended: Foreign service officers, international development coordinators, Arabic-language program assistants, and community outreach coordinators use developing Arabic proficiency for basic professional interactions, community communication, and continued advanced language training.
prerequisites: AB 103 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Chinese IV
courseDescription: Reviews and reinforces the language skills developed throughout Chinese I, II, and III while helping students reach intermediate-low proficiency. Students strengthen practical Chinese speaking, listening, reading, and writing for continued study and increasingly independent communication.
whyRecommended: Foreign service officers, international business coordinators, China research assistants, and localization project coordinators use developing Chinese proficiency to support basic professional communication, regional research, and multilingual projects.
prerequisites: CI 103 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Intermediate Italian II
courseDescription: Reviews and reinforces the Italian skills developed in IT 101 through IT 103 while moving students toward intermediate proficiency in reading, writing, speaking, listening, and cultural knowledge. Students work with authentic readings, Italian discussions, film clips, and required language-laboratory activities.
whyRecommended: Italian travel operations coordinators, study-abroad assistants, cultural exchange staff, and localization assistants use intermediate Italian to communicate with partners, interpret routine materials, and support Italy-focused programs.
prerequisites: IT 103 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Comprehensive Beginning French
courseDescription: Compresses the content of FR 101 and FR 102 into one intensive semester covering French reading, listening, speaking, writing, grammar, and cultural knowledge. Students attend six class sessions each week, complete required laboratory study, and prepare to begin intermediate French.
whyRecommended: International program assistants, travel coordinators, cultural exchange staff, and community outreach assistants use the French foundation developed here when supporting French-speaking participants and preparing for intermediate language training.
prerequisites: Open to students beginning a second modern language or placed into FR 101 or FR 102
Closed to students who completed FR 101, FR 102, or equivalent

title: Comprehensive Beginning Spanish
courseDescription: Compresses the content of SN 101 and SN 102 into one intensive semester covering Spanish reading, listening, speaking, writing, grammar, and cultural knowledge. Students attend six class sessions each week, complete required laboratory study, and prepare to enter intermediate Spanish.
whyRecommended: International program assistants, travel coordinators, community outreach staff, and education assistants use the Spanish foundation developed here when supporting Spanish-speaking participants and preparing for intermediate language training.
prerequisites: Open to students beginning a second modern language or placed into SN 102
Closed to students who completed SN 101, SN 102, or equivalent

title: Business French: A Functional Approach
courseDescription: Develops functional French for business settings while introducing the economic and professional environment of the French-speaking world. Students learn technical vocabulary, business idioms, cultural expectations, and the rules used to write formal business correspondence.
whyRecommended: International sales coordinators, export account coordinators, global marketing specialists, and French-language client service professionals use these skills to write correspondence, communicate with clients, and navigate Francophone business practices.

title: Contemporary Spanish Civilization and Culture
courseDescription: Examines Spain's historical, political, and cultural development from Francisco Franco's death in 1975 to the present. Students use Spanish-language readings, films, and music to analyze the transition to democracy, the cultural expansion of the 1980s, regional politics, and Spain's cultural diversity.
whyRecommended: Spain program coordinators, foreign service officers, Iberian market researchers, and cultural affairs specialists use this knowledge to interpret Spanish political developments, regional identities, media, and cultural expectations.
prerequisites: SN 203 or SN 217 or written permission of the instructor

title: History of the Spanish Language
courseDescription: Traces Spanish from its origins in spoken Latin through its development into the modern language. Students examine how historical events produced language changes and how literature contributed to the standardization of Spanish.
whyRecommended: Linguists, Spanish teachers, translators, and localization specialists use historical language analysis to explain word origins, recognize structural changes, and make informed translation and language-use decisions.
prerequisites: SN 203 or SN 217 or written permission of the instructor

title: U.S. History Since Reconstruction
courseDescription: Examines United States history from the Civil War through the country's development as an industrial and international power. Students analyze Reconstruction, immigration, industrialization, democratic reform, the world wars, the Great Depression, the Cold War, postwar culture, and modern social movements.
whyRecommended: Public historians, policy research analysts, museum educators, and social studies teachers use this historical framework to explain modern institutions, connect policies to their origins, and interpret major changes in American society.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Civil Rights Era
courseDescription: Examines the Black struggle for equality from disfranchisement in the 1890s through the civil rights conflicts of the 1960s and 1970s. Students analyze institutional and cultural barriers in the North and South and the organized strategies African Americans and their allies used to challenge them.
whyRecommended: Civil rights policy analysts, museum educators, public historians, and advocacy researchers use this knowledge to document discrimination, explain movement strategies, interpret legislation, and connect current policy debates to historical institutions.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Africa in the Age of Globalization
courseDescription: Examines African history since World War II through decolonization, the Cold War, independence, and the post-Cold War era of globalization. Students evaluate the development choices available to newly independent states and how colonial legacies constrained political, social, and economic progress.
whyRecommended: Africa policy analysts, international development specialists, country risk analysts, and NGO program officers use this historical context to assess development barriers, interpret government decisions, and design regionally informed programs.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Introduction to Modern Latin America
courseDescription: Surveys Latin American history from pre-Columbian societies to the present while examining political, social, and economic change across Central and South America. Students analyze the roles of Indigenous peoples, Africans, people of mixed ancestry, and women in forming regional identities, along with United States-Latin American relations and major regional trends.
whyRecommended: Latin America analysts, foreign service officers, international development specialists, and cultural affairs officers use this regional history to prepare country briefings, interpret U.S.-Latin American relations, and assess political and economic developments.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Law, Lawyers, and Litigants in European History
courseDescription: Traces European law and jurisprudence from Ancient Rome through the Enlightenment, including Roman legal compilations, canon law, the medieval ius commune, professional legal practice, and codification. Students examine how legal institutions interacted and how law both influenced and responded to social and cultural change.
whyRecommended: Legal researchers, law librarians, public historians, and attorneys use this historical foundation to trace legal doctrines, interpret institutional change, and explain how modern European legal systems developed.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: History of South Asia in the Twentieth Century
courseDescription: Examines twentieth-century South Asia with primary attention to India and additional coverage of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Burma. Students analyze colonial rule, nationalism, independence movements, Partition, religion, economic development, foreign policy, technological change, and regional cultural life.
whyRecommended: South Asia policy analysts, foreign service officers, international development specialists, and regional risk analysts use this history to prepare country briefings, interpret political divisions, and evaluate regional development and diplomatic issues.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Golden Age of Athens
courseDescription: Examines the political and cultural forces that shaped fifth-century Athens, including Athenian democracy, the Persian Wars, Pericles, imperial expansion, and the Peloponnesian War. Students evaluate how democratic institutions, military power, philosophy, and political conflict contributed to Athens' rise and decline.
whyRecommended: Classical historians, museum curators, civic education specialists, and archaeology program coordinators use this material to interpret democratic institutions, explain classical conflicts, and develop historically accurate educational content.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Gender, Race, and Class in Modern Europe
courseDescription: Examines modern European history from the French Revolution to the present through the experiences of women, people of color, workers, and the poor. Students analyze how gender, race, and class were used to regulate people and how marginalized groups resisted through feminism, labor conflict, anti-imperialism, migration, and other movements.
whyRecommended: European affairs researchers, migration policy analysts, museum curators, and public historians use this analysis to explain inequality, interpret social movements, and develop historically grounded policy and educational materials.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Introduction to the Modern Middle East
courseDescription: Surveys the Arab world, Turkey, and Iran from World War I to the present. Students examine imperialism, nationalism, modern state formation, Islamism, oil politics, the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, the Gulf Wars, and the 2011 Arab uprisings.
whyRecommended: Middle East policy analysts, foreign service officers, energy policy analysts, and international business risk analysts use this history to interpret regional conflicts, assess political risk, and explain how oil, nationalism, and state formation affect current decisions.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Black Death in Global Perspective
courseDescription: Examines the Black Death as a pandemic affecting Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East rather than as an exclusively European event. Students combine historical texts with evidence from paleobiology and archaeology to evaluate the plague's spread, regional responses, and political, religious, and social consequences.
whyRecommended: Public health historians, global health policy analysts, museum curators, and historical researchers use these skills to reconstruct disease outbreaks, compare societal responses, and communicate how pandemics reshape institutions.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The History of Modern China
courseDescription: Surveys major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in China from the early Qing dynasty through the People's Republic. Students use discussions, films, analytical papers, and a library project to connect historical transformations with modern Chinese society.
whyRecommended: China research analysts, foreign service officers, international business analysts, and cultural affairs specialists use this history to prepare country reports, evaluate market and political conditions, and interpret Chinese institutions and culture.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The First World War
courseDescription: Examines the origins, progression, and aftermath of the First World War across its European and global theaters. Students analyze soldiers' and civilians' experiences, colonial participation, home-front mobilization, gender, revolutions, border changes, international organizations, and the war's political and cultural memory.
whyRecommended: Military historians, foreign policy analysts, museum curators, and conflict researchers use this knowledge to explain the origins of international crises, interpret wartime evidence, and trace the borders and institutions created by global conflict.

title: Modern Iran Between Monarchy, Democracy, and Theocracy
courseDescription: Examines Iranian history from the Qajar dynasty through the Pahlavi monarchy, the 1979 Iranian Revolution, and the Islamic Republic. Students analyze modernization, European influence, oil politics, revolutionary change, Iran's relationship with the West, and its development as a regional power.
whyRecommended: Iran policy analysts, foreign service officers, energy policy analysts, and geopolitical risk analysts use this history to assess Iranian institutions, explain revolutionary politics, and evaluate regional and oil-related policy risks.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Psychology of Learning
courseDescription: Provides an in-depth examination of classical conditioning, instrumental learning, and cognitively based learning theories. Students apply these theories to human behavior and clinical situations involving behavior acquisition, reinforcement, and change.
whyRecommended: Behavior technicians, clinical research assistants, instructional designers, and learning and development specialists use these theories to design reinforcement plans, structure training, and evaluate how people acquire or change behaviors.

title: Sensation and Perception
courseDescription: This class follows sensory information from environmental stimulation through the sensory organs and into human perception. Students connect physiology to everyday experience by studying how emotion, learning, thought, and personal expectations can change what a person perceives.
whyRecommended: For UX researchers, human-factors specialists, occupational therapists, and perception researchers, the course builds the ability to separate what users physically sense from how attention and prior experience shape what they report.

title: Sleep, Circadian Rhythms, and Behavior
courseDescription: Students study how sleep and circadian rhythms are measured, regulated, and connected to cognition, performance, behavior, and physical and mental health. The course also applies sleep research to workplace scheduling, education, healthcare, public policy, and the treatment of sleep problems and disorders.
whyRecommended: Sleep technologists can apply the measurement concepts, while health psychologists, occupational-health specialists, and policy analysts use circadian evidence to address fatigue, scheduling, safety, and performance.

title: Life Span Development
courseDescription: This class tracks how people change from childhood through later adulthood from biological, behavioral, cognitive, and social perspectives. Students compare development across life stages and consider how changes in health, thinking, behavior, and relationships affect the support a person may need.
whyRecommended: A life-span perspective helps school counselors interpret age-appropriate behavior, human-services case managers plan support during major transitions, and gerontology professionals respond to changes in later adulthood.

title: Psychology of Personality
courseDescription: Students compare psychodynamic, trait, humanistic, and other major explanations of personality using research connected to each approach. They learn how personality develops, how different theories organize patterns of thought and behavior, and how to apply more than one framework when interpreting a person or case.
whyRecommended: Comparing personality frameworks gives counselors a disciplined foundation for case formulation and helps talent-development and market-research professionals interpret behavioral patterns without relying on stereotypes.

title: Introduction to Health Psychology
courseDescription: This course connects everyday behavior and environmental conditions to health and disease, with attention to diet, exercise, stress, smoking, weight, and pollutants. Students consider personal responsibility, behavior change, healthcare decisions, and nontraditional approaches to medicine without reducing health outcomes to individual choice alone.
whyRecommended: Public health educators can turn behavior-change evidence into prevention campaigns, while patient advocates and wellness coordinators use it to address stress, exercise, smoking, and adherence to health plans.

title: Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders
courseDescription: The course introduces major classes of psychoactive drugs, their effects, and the criteria used to identify substance-related and addictive disorders. Students compare treatment models and interventions, examine how addiction affects families, and consider the practical role of 12-step programs in recovery.
whyRecommended: Its practical diagnostic and intervention focus directly supports work in addiction counseling, behavioral-health intake, case management, and community recovery programs.

title: Multicultural Issues in Psychology
courseDescription: Students examine how culture and identity affect psychological research, professional practice, and the way behavior is interpreted. Through practice guidelines and structured self-reflection, they consider racial identity, sexual orientation, cultural assumptions, and the delivery of psychological services to diverse populations.
whyRecommended: Cultural self-reflection and practice guidelines prepare future counselors, school psychologists, inclusion specialists, and community-program staff to recognize bias and adapt services for diverse clients.

title: Psychology of Religion
courseDescription: This class approaches religion as a psychological experience that can be studied through learning, development, mental health, peak experiences, and social behavior. Students compare major psychological explanations of religious experience and evaluate research involving belief, prejudice, personal growth, and well-being.
whyRecommended: Chaplains and pastoral counselors gain language for recognizing the psychological dimensions of spiritual experience, while clinicians and researchers learn to study belief and well-being without treating religion as one uniform phenomenon.

title: Psychology of Gender
courseDescription: Students trace how gender develops through psychological processes, social expectations, media representation, parenting, relationships, sexuality, and ideas about masculinity. They also use feminism and intersectionality to evaluate research claims about sex differences and identify where study design or interpretation may introduce bias.
whyRecommended: In counseling, gender-equity advocacy, public relations, and user research, the course helps professionals evaluate gender claims and recognize when messages, services, or policies reinforce stereotypes.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
courseDescription: Students learn how individual and group psychological tests are designed, standardized, and validated before their scores can support real decisions. They apply measurement theory to intelligence, aptitude, and personality testing while examining what specific tests can diagnose and where their interpretations have limits.
whyRecommended: Assessment assistants, school psychologists, talent-selection specialists, and program evaluators rely on these measurement skills to choose instruments, interpret scores, and explain testing limitations responsibly.

title: Ethics in Psychology
courseDescription: Students work through professional and scientific ethics problems that arise in psychological research and practice. Using case studies, they apply ethical standards, identify competing responsibilities, compare possible responses, and defend decisions during seminar discussions.
whyRecommended: Clinical research coordinators, behavioral-health case managers, and future psychologists use this training to identify ethical risks, protect clients and participants, and document defensible professional decisions.

title: Theology and the Arts: A Global History
courseDescription: This course follows the changing relationship between Christian theology and the arts across two thousand years and multiple regions. Students interpret theological ideas in visual art, music, and architecture, consider how artists have challenged religious teachings, and apply their analysis during a museum visit.
whyRecommended: Museum educators, curators, arts writers, and sacred-space designers benefit from understanding how art and architecture communicate, reinterpret, or challenge theological ideas across cultures.

title: Women in the Christian Tradition
courseDescription: Students trace the contributions of women to Christianity through primary writings and historical research. Topics include women in the early church, medieval widows and abbesses, reformers, evangelical women, feminist critiques, and women's religious experiences in the United States.
whyRecommended: Archivists, museum educators, religious-studies researchers, and ministry leaders can use the course to recover overlooked sources and explain how women shaped Christian institutions and debates.

title: History and Storytelling in the Bible
courseDescription: This class compares the Bible's accounts of Israel, early Judaism, Jesus, and the early Christian church with evidence from other historical sources. Students learn to distinguish a text's historical claims from its rhetorical and theological purposes instead of treating every biblical narrative as modern historical reporting.
whyRecommended: Biblical researchers, editors, educators, and faith-based communicators need this source-comparison skill to explain where theological storytelling and historical evidence support, complicate, or challenge one another.

title: Christian Theology and World Religions
courseDescription: Students compare historical and contemporary Christian approaches to other religious traditions, with sustained attention to at least one non-Christian tradition. The course helps them identify genuine agreements and disagreements between traditions without reducing different religions to interchangeable beliefs.
whyRecommended: Interfaith coordinators, diplomats, religious-affairs analysts, and chaplains use comparative theological reasoning to discuss religious differences accurately and work across communities without relying on stereotypes.

title: Why Do We Suffer? Theological and Spiritual Perspectives on Suffering
courseDescription: Students compare Buddhist, Islamic, Jewish, Christian, philosophical, political, and musical responses to physical and emotional suffering. They evaluate whether particular beliefs and practices support healing, create additional harm, or fail to address what a suffering person actually needs.
whyRecommended: Chaplains, grief counselors, healthcare advocates, and trauma-informed ministry workers can draw on these perspectives when supporting people whose pain involves spiritual, cultural, and emotional questions.

title: Ethics: Immigration and Catholic Social Teaching
courseDescription: Students use Christian scripture, theological thinkers, and Catholic social teaching to evaluate the ethics of immigration. They apply those sources to public policy, economic interests, political responsibilities, and the treatment of migrants rather than discussing immigration only as an abstract moral issue.
whyRecommended: Immigration advocates, nonprofit policy staff, pastoral leaders, and public-interest lawyers gain a structured way to evaluate immigration policies, advocacy claims, and community responses through Catholic social ethics.

title: Worship, Culture, and Justice
courseDescription: Students study how worship practices interact with culture and how including or excluding cultural traditions affects religious communities. Using theology, liturgical texts, sociology of religion, and cultural anthropology, they evaluate worship among immigrants, racial minorities, people with disabilities, and communities in the United States and the majority world.
whyRecommended: Campus ministers, worship planners, community organizers, and inclusion specialists can use the course to evaluate who is represented, welcomed, or excluded when institutions design public religious practices.

title: Encounters between Christianity, Judaism, and Islam
courseDescription: Students compare medieval and contemporary encounters among Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, with particular attention to Jewish responses to Christian and Islamic claims of Abrahamic heritage. They analyze disagreements about God, creation, revelation, prophets, human nature, and the limits of religious language without treating the three traditions as interchangeable.
whyRecommended: Interfaith program coordinators, chaplains, religious-affairs analysts, and researchers use this kind of precise comparison to facilitate dialogue while accurately representing where religious communities agree and disagree.

title: War, Health, and Peacebuilding
courseDescription: Students study how armed conflict damages individual health, public-health systems, and access to medical care, then consider how healthcare work can contribute to peacebuilding. The course connects war ethics, global health, religious responses, and reconciliation so students can evaluate support for communities recovering from conflict.
whyRecommended: The course prepares humanitarian health officers, peacebuilding coordinators, and global-health analysts to connect damage to health systems with ethical recovery, reconciliation, and community-support strategies.

title: Bioethics and Social Justice
courseDescription: Students apply social-justice principles to decisions in biomedical research, healthcare policy, and medical practice. Using theological sources and cases ranging from Henrietta Lacks to the COVID-19 pandemic, they identify who receives medical benefits, who bears risks, and how institutions should respond to unequal outcomes.
whyRecommended: Clinical research coordinators, healthcare policy analysts, compliance professionals, and forensic scientists rely on these skills when reviewing medical practices for fairness, informed consent, institutional responsibility, and defensible ethical standards.

title: Religion, Poverty, and American Health Care
courseDescription: This course shows how religious institutions have shaped American healthcare and how poverty, social identity, and religious difference affect access to care. Students examine Catholic hospitals, nonprofit organizations, and partnerships between religious communities and medical agencies to determine whether limited resources are being used in culturally sensitive and sustainable ways.
whyRecommended: Hospital community-benefit staff, patient advocates, faith-based nonprofit managers, and public-health coordinators can apply this material when building programs for low-income and religiously diverse communities.

title: Character Ethics: Becoming Good
courseDescription: Students compare major Christian approaches to ethics while focusing on how habits and character shape moral choices. Case studies ranging from war to social media require them to explain why an action is good, what kind of person it encourages someone to become, and how repeated choices build character.
whyRecommended: Whether setting workplace standards, advising students, leading a ministry, or designing leadership training, professionals use character-based reasoning to translate broad values into expectations for everyday conduct.

title: The Ethics of War and Peace
courseDescription: Students compare holy-war traditions, just-war reasoning, and pacifism across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic history. They then evaluate twentieth-century Catholic peace efforts and contemporary initiatives to determine how religious ideas are translated into decisions about violence, restraint, reconciliation, and peace.
whyRecommended: Peacebuilding specialists, humanitarian policy analysts, military-ethics researchers, and interfaith mediators apply these frameworks when assessing whether force is justified and what responsible reconciliation requires afterward.

title: The Holocaust and Jewish Law
courseDescription: Students study how Jewish communities interpreted and continued observing Jewish law under genocidal persecution during the Holocaust. The course first explains how Jewish law develops and functions, then uses historical debates to show how people made religious and ethical decisions under conditions designed to destroy communal life.
whyRecommended: Holocaust museum educators, religious archivists, genocide researchers, and Jewish studies coordinators need this historical and legal grounding to explain responses to persecution without flattening the experiences or decisions of affected communities.
